# FOS Rule Entry-Point Code Reading Notes

`src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php` is still the best file to open first in this set of FOS rule notes. What is recorded here are code-reading reference points for the file header and extension class; they have not been organized into a complete call chain from configuration all the way to the client. When encountering names in the class body, first disambiguate them using the qualified names already written in this file.

The local structure of the file can first be sketched as follows:

```text
src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php
        |
        +-- namespace FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\DependencyInjection;
        |
        +-- class FOSElasticaExtension extends Extension
        |
        +-- File-header imports
              |-- Elastica\\Client as ElasticaClient
              |-- FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Elastica\\Client
              |-- FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Manager\\RepositoryManagerInterface
              `-- Symfony\\Component\\Config\\FileLocator
```

The namespace appears on line 12:

```php
namespace FOS\ElasticaBundle\DependencyInjection;
```

This reference point corresponds to the `DependencyInjection` directory containing the file. Line 27 gives the first type to identify along the current path:

```php
class FOSElasticaExtension extends Extension
```

`FOSElasticaExtension` is the class name already located in the file, and `Extension` is the parent class explicitly written in the class declaration. When reading the class body, distinguish these two names from the imports: the inheritance relationship comes from the declaration line, while the client, manager, and locator are, for now, only name-based entry points provided by the file header. Do not collapse them into a statement such as "the extension depends on the client", as that would conflate a relationship confirmed by the syntax with usage relationships in the class body that still need to be checked.

The client imports in the file header are the easiest part to misread in this review:

```php
use Elastica\Client as ElasticaClient;
use FOS\ElasticaBundle\Elastica\Client;
```

The first line aliases the external `Elastica\Client` as `ElasticaClient`. The second line comes from `FOS\ElasticaBundle\Elastica` and does not use an alias, so its short name is `Client`. Therefore, when `ElasticaClient` appears in the class body, refer back to the first line; when `Client` appears on its own, refer back to the second line. Having both is not a duplicate import, and they must not both be referred to simply as "client" in notes or search results. This distinction is supported only by the file header itself; whether they are used in parameters, properties, or method bodies should only be recorded after the relevant occurrences are actually found in the class body.

The other two imports lead the reader in different directions. The full name of `RepositoryManagerInterface` shows that it is the name of an interface under `FOS\ElasticaBundle\Manager`; what can currently be confirmed is the interface import itself, and this line alone cannot be used to fill in a concrete manager, return value, or call sequence. `FileLocator` comes from `Symfony\Component\Config` and belongs to a different group of objects from those in the preceding bundle and Elastica namespaces. When encountering this short name, check it together with nearby filenames, directory arguments, or exception branches; do not infer path rules from the import line alone.

An early draft recorded only the class name and four imports, and the reading order also stopped at "start from the file header". This review has not removed that assessment of the entry point; instead, it has made the disambiguation between the two `Client` names explicit and left anything not yet located in the source code as it was. This lets later readers start with the namespace, then the class declaration, then the imports, without first having to guess the entry point based on other Elastica or Manager names in the directory.

When checking the code, first search the `FOSElasticaExtension` class body for `ElasticaClient`, `Client`, `RepositoryManagerInterface`, and `FileLocator`. When `Client` is found, record the fully qualified name rather than just the short name; when an aliased name is found, preserve the `Elastica\Client as ElasticaClient` relationship as well. If an import does not appear in the class body, still keep a record stating "import seen, usage location unverified", rather than filling the gap with a class of the same name from elsewhere.

This also explains the boundary between this page and DOC-02. DOC-02 records the FOS callback relationship; this page starts only from the namespace, inheritance declaration, and imports of `FOSElasticaExtension`. Both pages may contain the FOS object name, but the reference point here is the file entry point, and this entry-point description does not expand on the callback process.

The first-use locations of the four imports in the class body are still unverified; whether `FileLocator` establishes a standalone file-location rule, and exactly what kind of declaration `RepositoryManagerInterface` appears as in the class body, also remain open questions in this local record.

versions.body:
# Client request compatibility decision record

Initially, two topics from the 2026.09 compatibility window were recorded together: client request compatibility and conditional persistence scheduling. They were put in the same decision record not because they were known to share an implementation, but to avoid treating persistence timing as an established side conclusion while investigating the request entry point.

At the time, `src/Elastica/Client.php` was the only object we could tie to code. Near the top of the file, `Elastica\Client as BaseClient`, `Elastica\Exception\ClientException`, `Elastica\Index as BaseIndex`, and `Elastica\Request` were visible. These names were enough for subsequent notes to distinguish the bundle-side client, underlying client, index object, request object, and exception type; they did not establish a call sequence.

The initial discussion compared two approaches.

- Treat both request compatibility and persistence scheduling as transport issues and make an initial unified assessment based on the client class.
- Keep the client class as a checkpoint near the request entry point; document persistence scheduling separately and defer judgment until the actual path is available.

We chose the latter. The cost was that the material on both sides would not be complete in the same pass; the benefit was not inferring from the import list that a conditional branch had already been taken. The presence of `BaseIndex` could only establish that the index object was within the scope of this code reading; it could not substitute for verifying the actual index lookup.

At the time, there was still one working hypothesis: if the request entry point had not disappeared as the underlying client changed, compatibility issues would probably show up first at the client boundary. This hypothesis only helped set the order for follow-up checks. There was not yet enough evidence to show that it covered index lookup, much less conditional persistence scheduling.

So we kept two lines of investigation: for request issues, first go back to the area around `Client.php` to identify the objects; for conditional persistence, wait only for a record of what the entry point returns or throws in practice. Don't turn "appeared in the same compatibility window" into "had the same cause."

Still to capture: the objects the request actually passes through; what is observed from persistence scheduling when the condition is met and when it is not.

# Client Request Compatibility Decision Record

This record initially treated the 2026.09 compatibility window as a narrowly scoped client issue. A later review found that client request compatibility and conditional persistence scheduling appearing in the same round of requirements does not mean they should be handled by the same class, supported by the same kind of evidence, or covered by the same conclusion. The original decision to separate them still stands; this update only adds the boundaries that could be established from the client file and the review at the time.

## Initial Approach

The starting point is still `src/Elastica/Client.php`. The directly visible objects are `BaseClient`, `ClientException`, `BaseIndex`, and `Request`. The original record described this file as being near the entry point for request compatibility, rather than assigning persistence scheduling to it. That wording was not elegant at the time, but it was closer to the evidence actually available than "the client is responsible for all compatibility."

One shortcut considered at the time was to explain all observations through transport differences in the underlying client, then infer indexing and scheduling from the same place. It kept the scope very narrow and read smoothly. However, mentioning both `BaseIndex` and `Request` in the file does not establish when the condition is met, who triggers scheduling, whether scheduling completes, or even who makes the request. The original decision not to compress these three things into a single chain remains valid.

Another approach considered was to record only `BaseClient` and treat all other names as implementation details. This approach was not adopted. The reason was not that `BaseIndex` or `Request` had been proven to have some fixed behavior, but that both are among the neighboring objects visible in this file; omitting these objects entirely from later investigations could easily lead to "the client is still usable" being misrecorded as "the index and requests have also been checked."

## Review Addendum

The counterexample recorded during the review was simple: the request entry point still being able to accept objects does not automatically answer whether conditional persistence has been scheduled. It did not provide the complete execution chain, but it was enough to overturn a shortcut in working habits: assuming scheduling is fine simply because the entry point looks normal.

The assessment is therefore split into two questions.

1. On the request side, check only which neighboring names between the bundle-side client and the underlying client, request objects, and index objects need further verification.
2. conditional persistence scheduling requires the content returned or thrown on its own path; without this, it can only be recorded as not yet confirmed.

This does not split the two requirements into unrelated matters. Users may still encounter both during a single use, but this decision does not allow the client file to stand in for evidence from the scheduling path. If only a request sample is available, the record can stop at the request boundary; if only evidence from conditional persistence is available, start with that evidence rather than circling back to `Client.php` to look for an explanation that can substitute for the result.

## Earlier Assessment Retained During the Follow-up Review

During the follow-up review, the client file was reopened, confirming that the four object names originally recorded were correct. The review did not identify the request caller or the execution point for conditional persistence scheduling. The earlier assessment below was therefore retained with its original meaning to help explain why further inferences based on it were later abandoned:

> As long as the `BaseClient` side can continue accepting requests, index lookups and conditional persistence scheduling can broadly be handled under the same compatibility conclusion; address transport first, then the remaining differences.

At the time, this statement was only a working hypothesis, not a verified decision. It mistook "objects appear near each other in the same file" for "behaviors will occur together." The import at the top of the file can help identify the objects being examined, but cannot establish the call order or prove that a condition has already led to persistence.

At the time, some favored strengthening this statement, for example by directly changing "can accept requests" to "the entire compatibility window can continue to be used." This change was not adopted. The available evidence did not establish the operational scope of the entire window; turning a convenient generalization into a broad promise would mislead later readers into thinking that scheduling and index lookups already had equal support.

## Decision for This Round

The decision is to maintain two independent verification tracks rather than add a blanket transport conclusion for the compatibility window.

- `src/Elastica/Client.php` remains the local navigation point for client request compatibility. The record may discuss the boundaries among client, request, and index objects.
- conditional persistence scheduling is not to be inferred from the import or names in this file. If later runtime evidence contains only a request error, it cannot be recorded as a persistence scheduling result.
- If a user report provides an actual path, preserve the content actually returned or thrown by that path. When the original content is unavailable, writing "unconfirmed" is more accurate than adding a guess of success or failure.

This decision did not select the "unified compatibility layer" approach. The reason is not that the approach is necessarily wrong, but that the available evidence supports only the local relationships in the client file and cannot support combining the request entry point, index lookups, and persistence scheduling into a single causal chain. New evidence from execution paths may later change the assessment on one track; until then, a single heading should not be used to merge the conclusions prematurely.

## Objects Still Unresolved at the Boundaries

conditional persistence scheduling needs an entry point that provides visibility into the conditional branch. No such entry point has been found here so far. The next addendum should provide the return value or exception from the actual path, rather than continue adding explanations of `Client.php` terminology.

The index object also has a separate gap. The introduction of `BaseIndex` is enough to show that it falls within the reading scope of the client compatibility track, but not enough to establish its specific behavior under different transport API. This issue remains on the request compatibility track for now and is not merged with the scheduling issue.

`ClientException` is likewise retained as a visible object, not presented as evidence of a particular compatibility failure. An exception type appearing in the dependencies and a particular user path actually throwing that exception are two different things. Without a path or the content returned or thrown, an incident cannot be reconstructed from the name.

This record remains useful for looking back at why the client entry point and conditional scheduling were separated at the time; it does not provide a complete runtime explanation.

This page began as a very narrowly scoped client record, and was later used repeatedly to explain two closely related but distinct terms: client request compatibility and conditional persistence scheduling. The earliest file that can be reliably located is `src/Elastica/Client.php`. The initial record has no complete call graph, nor any runtime output that can be traced step by step. It only notes a few names near the top of the file:`Elastica\Client as BaseClient`,`Elastica\Exception\ClientException`,`Elastica\Index as BaseIndex` and `Elastica\Request`.

The assessment at the time was straightforward: request and index objects both appeared near the client class, so the file could serve as a reference point for client request compatibility. The "reference point" here was never an "implementation location". It means that when someone later returns with a question about request compatibility, they can first check whether the bundle-side client, underlying client, request object and index object were referred to interchangeably in the record; it does not mean this file already shows how these objects run in sequence.

The same initial record also placed conditional persistence scheduling near the title. That was not because the client class was known to perform scheduling, but because users describing compatibility often put "whether requests can still get in" and "whether persistence is scheduled once the conditions are met" into the same round of feedback. The initial choice was not to create another broad compatibility layer; the client file would first serve as a navigation aid on the request side, while the scheduling side would wait for concrete paths to emerge.

There were two options on the table at the time.

| Option at the time | Apparent benefit at the time | Gap already visible at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classify requests, indexes and scheduling together as transport compatibility | A centralized reference location, a short record | Would mistake adjacent names in the file for an execution relationship |
| Record the client entry point and scheduling observations separately | Would not infer conditional branches from import | The two sides could not immediately be combined into a conclusion in the same round |

The initial decision selected the second option. The decision is narrow in scope: this page does not substitute client files for the scheduling path, nor does it turn the appearance of `BaseIndex` into a claim that index lookup has been confirmed. It does not assert that the two paths must be completely separate in the implementation, much less prescribe when persistence should occur.

There was also a working assumption at the time: if the request entry point did not disappear as the underlying client changed, compatibility issues would probably surface first at the client boundary. This assumption was used only to decide where to look first; there were not yet any counterexamples, nor was there evidence that it covered index lookup or conditional persistence. The early notes presented this premise more neatly than the actual material warranted, which is also why a record of the corrections later needed to be retained.

## The counterexample left by the initial review

The most useful counterexample in the review addendum was brief: the fact that the request entry point can continue to accept objects does not automatically answer whether conditional persistence has been scheduled. It did not provide a complete execution chain, but it was enough to overturn the convenient judgment that "if the entry point looks normal, we can also assume scheduling is fine."

After this counterexample, the early notes split verification into two passes. The first addressed only the object names encountered by the bundle client: the reading boundary within which each of `BaseClient`, `Request`, `BaseIndex`, and `ClientException` falls. The second addressed only the actual entry point for conditional persistence: if nothing is returned or thrown, do not record success, do not record failure, and do not record a scheduling order.

These two verification passes do not require a full set of checks for every user report. When someone brings only a sample request, the record can end near the client entry point; when someone brings only observations of conditional persistence, the investigation should follow that entry point directly, rather than circling back to the client class to find an answer that can substitute for the results actually observed. They may ultimately point to the same usage path, but appearing together in the context of the same requirement does not mean they already share a cause.

The review also left a constraint on wording: do not turn "the client is still present" into "all related behavior is still present." The former is at most an observation about objects and entry points, while the latter already encompasses index lookup, scheduling conditions, and callers that have not yet been seen. This constraint remained useful later on, especially when old links took readers only as far as `Client.php`.

## The old route, retained in place

The passage below was among the most frequently cited in the early documentation, and also among the easiest to misuse. It is retained here so that old troubleshooting links can still explain why attention was focused on `BaseClient` at the time.

> If the bundle-side client can continue to handle requests, index lookup and conditional persistence scheduling can generally be treated as covered by the same compatibility conclusion; look at transport first, and address the other differences afterward.

This passage is now deprecated. At the object level, it placed `BaseClient`, `BaseIndex`, and `Request` on the same page, but at the behavioral level, it skipped the supporting material required for index lookup and conditional scheduling individually. Subsequent review did not establish that this approach was viable, but instead made its gaps clearer: the import statements at the top of the file can only help identify adjacent objects, not establish the call order, much less prove that a particular condition has already led to persistence.

The old approach is not being removed from historical versions, not because it can still serve as operational steps, but because some people still reach this page through old troubleshooting records. When arriving via an old link, stop at this marker and do not copy this passage into a new compatibility conclusion. It describes the simplified method used at the time, not the current assessment of changes to transport API.

Another equally invalid formulation is to describe `ClientException` outright as "the exception for request compatibility failures." Seeing this exception type in the file only shows that it is one of the client file's direct dependencies; without a specific path and what was actually thrown, the exception name cannot be retroactively attributed to a particular user incident. This old formulation was never documented separately, but it appeared in several verbal summaries, so it is retained here as well to explain its problems.

## 2024 review: Not seeing it does not mean lower risk

The later review reopened `src/Elastica/Client.php` and confirmed that the four object names originally extracted had been recorded correctly. The review also retained the original view of the file's role: the client file is suitable for checking request-side object boundaries, but should not be described as the home of conditional persistence scheduling.

The review did not identify the request caller, did not find a branch from which the scheduling conditions could be determined, and did not provide any output that could establish the persistence outcome. These gaps were not filled at the time. Someone suggested summarizing this as "The client has not changed, so the scheduling risk is lower," but that suggestion was not adopted. The review actually reached only a narrower conclusion: the available file material was insufficient to assess scheduling.

After this review, a very specific reading practice was added to the record: when a description contains all three terms request, index, and persistence, first ask whether they refer to the same object relationship, the same call path, or merely appear on the same requirements card. If only the last answer applies, they should not then be compressed into a single causal sentence.

This practice also changed the previous sequence for tracing back through the material. Previously, some people would start with `BaseClient` and treat `Request`, `BaseIndex`, and persistence as natural follow-ups all along the way. After the review, the client file is used only for identifying names and navigating to adjacent objects; index lookup requires its own supporting material on behavior; conditional scheduling, in particular, cannot be judged positively or negatively merely because the names are adjacent.

## A consolidated formulation that was not adopted

To make the explanation of the compatibility window shorter, the following consolidated formulation was tried:

1. Use the client file to show that requests can still enter.
2. Treat index lookup as the natural next step after that entry point.
3. Treat conditional persistence scheduling as the outcome at the end of the same chain.

The issue is not the first step's value to readers. `Client.php` does give the request side an object location to refer back to. The problem lies between the second and third steps: the fact that `BaseIndex` appears among the direct dependencies only shows that the index object is an adjacent object that this page must not omit; it cannot extend "an identifiable index object" into "index lookup under different transport API has been confirmed", much less establish that persistence scheduling has run.

This combined framing was therefore dropped. This does not, conversely, mean that client compatibility and scheduling are completely unrelated. More precisely: whether the two are related must be established by actual paths, not by the arrangement of names in a class file. Keeping them in the same decision record preserves this separation, rather than declaring that they belong to the same implementation location.

At one point, it was suggested that the two phrases in the title be split into two records with no cross-references, on the grounds that this would avoid misinterpretation. This suggestion was not adopted either. If they were separated completely, later readers would instead lose sight of why they had initially been combined, as well as the historical context in which "the request entry point is working normally" was incorrectly extended to the scheduling outcome. Keeping them on the same page but assessing them separately was therefore the more appropriate compromise at the time.

## Changes after field regression testing was added to the record

In 2025, ATL-201 was moved back into the review stage. The card's initial description called for adding repository tests based on user-reported examples of client request compatibility, and preserving the current failure text or output bytes. It also explicitly continued to use the public spelling `Elastica`, which should be searched for exactly as written during investigation and review.

This requirement changed how this page handles request-side material. If request reports come in later, the priority is to retain the material from the field, rather than first summarizing transport differences using the old approach. Failure text or output bytes can show what was actually seen at the time; a statement that "it should be a client compatibility issue" cannot. The existing card description does not provide that text or output, so this page does not invent any failure symptoms.

Subsequent records for ATL-201 still retain "one point remains unconfirmed". This statement does not include an object, path, or output sufficient to reach a firm conclusion, so it cannot be expanded into a specific fault or treated as counterevidence to the current conclusion about the client. It only shows that the review had not reached closure at the time. The card's change history, from work beginning to a review being requested, records progress on the work, not proof of behavior.

ATL-218 keeps a separate record of regression testing for conditional persistence in the user's environment. It first had a baseline record and then moved into an in-progress state; the card requires running conditional persistence scheduling through the current public entry point and recording only what this path actually returns or throws. Here, "only record" has a very narrow scope: it provides no successful samples, no exception text, and no scheduling sequence.

Therefore, ATL-218 can only serve as a navigation point for scheduling in the user's environment. Its baseline record cannot be interpreted as a positive result or as a negative result. Nor is it valid to describe the card's move into an in-progress state as "persistence has been scheduled"; that would conflate work status with the execution path.

These two cards share the context of the compatibility window, but they do not share a verified call chain. ATL-201 points to additional evidence for request compatibility, while ATL-218 points to regression testing of conditional persistence in the user's environment. If material from the same usage path becomes available later, we can then determine whether a shared boundary exists; until then, this page maintains two separate records.

## An explicit change of position during review

Earlier discussions often made the overly broad statement that "the client is still a layer over Elastica". This phrasing is convenient, but makes it easy to overlook the fact that the request entry point and the index object are two public surfaces that must be verified separately. The later correction did not expand the discussion to all Elastica behavior, but instead limited this page to judgments supportable within the topic of client compatibility.

After the correction, the client file serves three purposes on this page:

- It preserves the naming relationship between the bundle-side client and `BaseClient`.
- It makes `Request` and `BaseIndex` adjacent objects that must not be overlooked during verification.
- It reminds readers that `ClientException` is a directly visible exception type, but the file header itself does not indicate which path would trigger it.

The third point was previously summarized as "a client exception means a request compatibility failure". That summary no longer applies. An exception type being visible in the dependencies and a particular user path actually throwing it are two different things. If later material contains only an exception name, with no corresponding entry point or output, it should not be retroactively recorded as a compatibility incident.

Another change of position during review concerned "the index object is already present, so index lookup does not need to be listed separately". The name `BaseIndex` is enough to make index lookup something that must be revisited, but not enough to declare that its behavior across transport API is already stable. The client file has not resolved this gap, and it should still be distinguished from the scheduling gap.

## Current Reading Branches

The diagram below shows only the current verification branches on this page; it does not indicate any execution order among requests, indexing, and scheduling. The two starting points are placed side by side to prevent the old approach from once again treating the entry point for reading about the client as proof of conditional persistence.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ClientReview
    ClientReview --> RequestEntry
    ClientReview --> IndexLookup
    [*] --> PersistenceObservation
    PersistenceObservation --> RuntimeResult
    RequestEntry --> [*]
    IndexLookup --> [*]
    RuntimeResult --> [*]
```

In the diagram, ClientReview corresponds to the object-level checks near `src/Elastica/Client.php`; RequestEntry and IndexLookup retain the reading scope for the request entry point and index lookup, respectively. PersistenceObservation indicates that evidence for conditional persistence scheduling must be obtained from its own public entry point, while RuntimeResult refers only to what that path actually returns or throws. The diagram does not connect ClientReview to PersistenceObservation, because the current material does not support that edge.

As of this addendum, this page maintains the decision to record compatibility assessments by object boundary and does not reinstate the earlier blanket attribution to transport. On the request side, checks can be made across the bundle client, the request entry point, and index lookup; conditional persistence scheduling must be supported by what is actually returned or thrown in its own context. For the same user report, two records can be created first, followed by a check for a shared path; a shared cause must not be assumed in advance just because both fall within the same compatibility window.

The current requirement to retain here is as follows: The bundle client remains an Elastica client and exposes a supported request entry point; index lookup returns an index object across transport API generations.

This statement addresses only the compatibility requirements for the bundle client, the request entry point, and index lookup. It does not declare that conditional persistence scheduling has been verified, nor does it define success criteria for scheduling conditions. If the only material available on site is at the client layer, at most the first part of the checks can be completed; the scheduling issue must still be observed through its own public entry point.

## Where This Connects to the Interface Review

The public shape of request event and service resource loading are discussed separately in the interface review at PHP-DOC-11. This page does not repeat the solution comparison there. There is only one constraint at the point where the two pages connect: the compatibility check at the request entry should not casually be used to draw conclusions about the public shape of request event; the service resource loading issue also cannot serve as corroborating evidence that conditional persistence has already occurred.

This constraint was added later. Early records treated "the request can get in" as a sufficiently broad statement, making it easy for readers to fold event and service resource issues into client conclusions. We are retaining the old wording, but subsequent additions should first make clear whether they are checking the client, event shape, resource loading, or the scheduling context. Adjacent objects can guide the search, but they cannot automatically merge ownership.

## Adjacent Issues Not Yet Split Out

The object boundary for index lookup has now been fixed in the current requirements, but how to identify the corresponding index lookup from a concrete user path is still not recorded on this page. This gap should not be filled by guesswork.

The gap in conditional persistence scheduling is more specific: it requires a reproducible public entry point and the content that entry point actually returns or throws. ATL-218 is an existing navigation point; until actual runtime content is available, its baseline record should not be interpreted as a positive or negative result.

Another point remains easy to confuse: if someone sees only client objects while tracing transport API generations, they should not write back "scheduling is consistent in every generation". This page does not make that conclusion, and the retained old route cannot provide it either. The current requirement on the request side and the unconfirmed status on the scheduling side can coexist; one need not replace the other.

## Legacy Examples Appendix: Still Retained, but Do Not Follow

**Legacy Example One: Inferring the Full Chain from import.**

Earlier, people would see `BaseClient`, `BaseIndex`, and `Request` appear together and write out the sequence "from request to index and then to persistence". This is shorthand for communication, not a call fact established from the files. This example is deprecated; it remains here because old troubleshooting notes once used this terminology. When tracing back using the old terminology, break it back down into three layers: the client, the index object, and the scheduling context.

**Legacy Example Two: Summarizing the Observed State with transport First.**

Another old practice was to first write "transport compatibility" and then force any request or scheduling phenomena into that heading. This makes the record look complete, but hides which parts have only object navigation and which have actual output. This example is no longer a starting point for new records; if new material concerns only the request entry, write only the request entry.

**Legacy Example Three: Treating Card Advancement as a Runtime Conclusion.**

The ATL-201 and ATL-218 that appeared later can easily lead readers to mistakenly believe that a card entering review or processing means the corresponding action already has a result. This example should not be followed either. The cards help readers find user reports, avenues for gathering additional evidence, and entry points to the environment in question; they do not replace the failure text, output bytes, return value, or exception from that entry point.

The appendix does not replace the current decision. It preserves the old reading path and the reasons it is no longer valid. When tracing back to `src/Elastica/Client.php` through the old links, readers can still see here why that file was chosen as the entry point for the client-side topic, and should also see why it cannot provide the required proof for conditional persistence scheduling.

# Request Event API Trial Plan

There is already `PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber` next to the pagination entry point, but it handles the pager's `ItemsEvent`, so it shouldn't be used directly as a template for a public request-layer API. This round, we'll look at request events and PHP service resources in the same compatibility trial: the former needs to provide callers with a stable object before and after a request, while the latter must not break existing user paths because of changes in how resources are loaded.

First, compare two approaches.

- Continue exposing the existing pagination events and attach request-related data to them.
- Keep the pagination subscriber limited to pagination adaptation, and introduce separate request lifecycle events.

The first approach is a smaller change, but pager inputs, query objects, and transport requests aren't all at the same layer; callers who only want to change the path or query would be forced to depend on pagination timing. The second requires defining the event object's minimum set of fields, but keeps request compatibility within its own boundary. We currently favor the second approach.

PHP service resources do not need to be converted to another resource format at this stage. The trial will only check whether existing PHP service resources can still be loaded; if users have to rewrite their service declarations, that is not an acceptable outcome within the compatibility window.

Material still needed:

1. Exactly which inputs callers need to read or override before a request is sent.
2. Whether exceptions should be passed out through the same object when a request fails.
3. Whether the shortest PHP service resource example can be loaded repeatedly.

If the event shape can only be inferred from the pager, or resource loading requires additional caller configuration, we'll withdraw this trial and keep the existing entry point for now.

# Request Event Interface Trial Plan

After review, the first change is to correct a shortcut in the initial draft: the pagination subscriber is a relevant place to look, not a basis for implementing transport events. The local relationships in its file are limited to these:

```php
use FOS\ElasticaBundle\Paginator\PaginatorAdapterInterface;
use FOS\ElasticaBundle\Paginator\PartialResultsInterface;
use Knp\Component\Pager\Event\ItemsEvent;
use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\EventSubscriberInterface;

class PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber implements EventSubscriberInterface
```

This shows that `PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber` connects Elastica's pagination adapter to Knp's `ItemsEvent`. It helps rule out the approach of "exposing pager events directly as request events," but it doesn't establish what fields the request object already has, nor can it define exception boundaries for request failure paths.

The review narrowed the options to a standalone request lifecycle object. The public object should not carry `ItemsEvent` or require callers to know about `PaginatorAdapterInterface` or `PartialResultsInterface`. The request layer should retain only the request information callers actually need; the pagination subscriber stays in its adapter role. The trade-off is maintaining a set of event classes rather than just adding a subscription callback. That cost is acceptable because mixing objects from the two layers would leave future callers unable to tell whether what they receive represents a query, pagination, or an actual request.

The default content type remains part of the trial, rather than something each caller has to supply. What's needed here is stable default behavior, not header selection tucked into pagination configuration. The failure event's public shape should also belong to the same family as those of the before and after events; the initial draft didn't make this clear.

The conclusion on the PHP service resource is limited: existing user paths can use this resource type, and the trial will not be used to rework service discovery. The review checks only two things: whether the resource can be processed, and whether the same example remains usable when processed again. If passing those checks requires users to switch to a different resource representation, that should be treated as an out-of-scope change.

No decision yet on whether the event object should handle all transport details. path, query, the default content type, and the failure object are what this round needs to settle; authentication, retries, and client construction remain in their respective calling layers. Once the minimal caller example and the resource example both run successfully, decide whether to finalize the object names.

# Request Event API Trial Plan

The first draft put too much weight on the pagination subscriber. The review version separated the pager from the request layer, but still left one gap too vague: callers need a predictable request object, not a description saying "you'll be notified when a request happens." This revision closes that gap without turning PHP service resource loading into a container refactor.

The old proposal is retained here to explain the direction we did not pursue. The original idea was to have `PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber` expose request notifications, since it already implemented `EventSubscriberInterface` and had `PaginatorAdapterInterface`, `PartialResultsInterface`, and Knp `ItemsEvent` nearby. This looked convenient at the interface level: the existing subscription points seemed like an easy place to add request information.

But that would conflate three otherwise distinct objects. `ItemsEvent` represents item processing during pagination; the adapter connects Elastica queries to the pager; transport requests have their own path, query, content type, and failure timing. Callers who only need to inspect or adjust a request should not have to understand paginated results first. The old proposal has therefore been dropped, and the subscriber remains only as pagination-adjacent code.

The source file's location is still useful, but only for confirming this layer's boundaries: `src/Subscriber/PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber.php` is in the `FOS\ElasticaBundle\Subscriber` namespace, and its class declaration is `class PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber implements EventSubscriberInterface`. Later changes to request events should not treat this file as the home for event classes or try to complete the public request API by changing its subscription to `ItemsEvent`.

The options compared for this trial are listed below.

| Option | What it retains | Reason not to adopt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add request data to pager events | Reuses existing subscription points | The request lifecycle leaks through the pagination lifecycle, leaving callers dependent on the wrong object |
| Provide only a pre-request notification | Minimal changes | Callers cannot use the same set of objects to handle completion and exceptions |
| Create a set of independent request events | Clear request boundaries | Requires maintaining event classes, but the compatibility scope can be explained and the change rolled back |

The third option is the current implementation target. "Independent" does not mean that all transport details must be public. It only requires that callers can see and use the request address and query parameters before the request, and identify what happened through the same lifecycle on completion or exception. Authentication, retries, client creation, and paginated results are outside these event objects; adding them would only increase the future compatibility burden.

The working contract is: PreElasticaRequestEvent exposes path and query accessors and defaults content type to application/json, with matching pre, post, and exception lifecycle event classes.

This entails two trade-offs. First, `path` and `query` are part of the public interface; internal pager objects are not used as substitute arguments. Call Fang Ke to work with them before the request, without having to guess whether the adapter has already converted the query into pagination items. Second, the event contract supplies the default content type, rather than leaving each caller to supply a potentially different default. The pre, post, and exception stages must be provided as a set; providing only a pre-event would push failure handling back onto each subscriber, while providing only a post-event would leave the exception path without an equivalent entry point.

The PHP service resource portion stays deliberately limited. The existing user workflow supports PHP service resource, which is enough to include it as a compatibility sample in this round; there is no supporting material for attributing service resource loading to the pagination subscriber or claiming that the resource-loading mechanism needs to be replaced. Testing the sample should be limited to verifying that the resource can be processed through the existing entry point and processing the same short example repeatedly. If the resource works the first time but fails when processed again, log the issue against the resource-loading path first; do not mask it with request event defaults.

Neither trial should be a prerequisite for the other. Passing the request event trial does not prove that PHP service resource loading is still reliable; passing the resource example does not prove that the exception lifecycle has a complete public interface. Both are in this proposal because they affect callers' upgrade costs during the compatibility window: one affects what callers can do when subscribing to requests, and the other affects whether existing service declarations can still enter the system.

Rollback conditions are handled separately as well: if `path` or `query` can only be obtained through `ItemsEvent`, back out the chosen placement of the independent public API and recheck which layer the request object lives in; if the default content type forces existing callers to override it explicitly on every request, roll back that default behavior as well; if PHP service resource must be rewritten into a different resource format before it can be processed, do not include that rewrite in this round's compatibility commitment. When rolling back, retain the pagination subscriber and the existing resource entry point; do not replace them with a temporary compatibility branch.

Whether event objects should expose more client request details is still undecided. No vague fields are being reserved for this. First complete the caller examples using path, query, the default content type, and the full set of lifecycle classes, then discuss additional information based on actual needs; fields without an example stay out of the public API.

# Template Rule Troubleshooting Tree

2023-12-14 During review, the investigation still starts at `src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php`. The issue name contains both template pattern and priority and backed enum normalization, but these two terms were only included in the same compatibility pass; that does not mean they share an execution path.

## The Initial Entry Has Not Been Removed

The search terms left on the old page are `config`, `template`, `indextemplateconfig`, and `empty`. They are useful for finding text on the configuration side, not field definitions. After opening the file, the only local excerpt that can still be confirmed is:

```php
namespace FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\DependencyInjection;

class FOSElasticaExtension extends Extension
```

The index also marks `FOS(type, line 12)` and `FOSElasticaExtension(type, line 27)`. These two locations lead back to the declaration site, but they do not show how the configuration object is formed or provide the values read for pattern or priority.

Earlier notes made "check extensions first" sound like an ownership assignment. We retain the original work order here, but narrow its meaning to a follow-up lookup entry point. When only a class declaration is visible, do not attribute the template anomaly to extension loading; when only file-header imports are visible, do not string adjacent dependencies into a call chain.

## File-side Notes

The dependencies visible in the file header are:

- `Elastica\\Client as ElasticaClient`
- `FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Elastica\\Client`
- `FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Manager\\RepositoryManagerInterface`
- `Symfony\\Component\\Config\\FileLocator`

During an earlier on-call shift, someone used the two Clients as if they had the same name. After review, retain just one reminder: distinguish them by their actual usage locations. `RepositoryManagerInterface` appears in the import list; that does not mean template sorting goes through the repository; `FileLocator` can only indicate that there is a nearby resource-location clue, not that a template configuration has been found.

## Post-review Branches

```text
A template-related symptom appears
├─ template is empty
│  └─ Record the input name; stop at the configuration side
├─ template is non-empty, but no configuration object is visible
│  └─ Record the last visible name and path; do not extend beyond this point yet
└─ Configuration object observed
   └─ Then look for the values actually read and nearby usage locations
```

"Stopping at the configuration side" is not a resolution; it only means the current excerpt ends here. Empty input cannot be taken directly as the default template; a non-empty input likewise cannot be taken directly to mean that a template has already been formed. If only an extension class declaration remains, record the namespace, class name, and path; do not infer an object from the import list.

The review comments for 2023-12-15 separate the entry point from the object: the file path is for tracing back, and the configuration name is for searching; neither can replace observing an object. If an actual object is seen later, record pattern, priority, or the enum value separately; if not, leave the gap.

## Keep the Two Topics Separate

template pattern and priority, as well as backed enum normalization, can still be navigated from the same page, but they are split into two lines during troubleshooting. When reporting only a template anomaly, first find the pattern and priority that actually appear; when reporting only an enum anomaly, first record the input, the visible conversion result, and the stopping point. Without these excerpts, do not borrow one topic's entry point for the other.

The topic for DOC-13 is raw finder interfaces and modern DBAL listener registration. It can serve as navigation for an adjacent compatibility record, but it cannot be used to fill in a template object that does not appear on this page.

## Old Conclusion

> Seeing `FOSElasticaExtension` is enough to attribute the template anomaly to this area.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Template Rule Anomalies

This page was originally just an on-call entry point. When template pattern and priority or backed enum normalization came up in an issue, people would first open `src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php`, then decide whether to look further into the configuration. The path was stable, but the conclusions were not: the filename could lead people to the PHP extension entry point, but the entry point alone could not establish whether the anomaly occurred during configuration loading, template object creation, or later use.

## Initial Notes: 2023-05-24

The earliest recorded procedure was brief. First search for `template`; if you see `empty`, go back to the configuration input; if it is not empty, open the extension file. The four commonly used search terms were `config`, `template`, `indextemplateconfig`, `empty`. No sample configuration was retained at the time, nor were any runtime snippets saved that could show changes in enum values.

There are two locations you can jump to directly in the file:

```php
namespace FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\DependencyInjection;

class FOSElasticaExtension extends Extension
```

The local references in the index are `FOS(type, line 12)` and `FOSElasticaExtension(type, line 27)`. They are useful in the editor, allowing troubleshooting to start from a stable location. The early working rule was "For configuration anomalies, check the extension first". This sentence is still here because it does describe the approach used at the time; it does not prove that this class alone determines template behavior, nor does it prove that backed enum normalization occurs here.

A very rough path was drawn at the time:

```text
Configuration input -> template -> indextemplateconfig -> FOSElasticaExtension
```

It later became clear that this arrow linked the input name, object name, and class declaration too hastily. The declaration did not show when the object was created, nor did it show the values of pattern or priority. This question was left open for the time being, and the initial notes were not revised to include the later assessment.

## On-Call Annotations Beside the File

Four dependencies in the file header were circled at the time:

- `Elastica\\Client as ElasticaClient`
- `FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Elastica\\Client`
- `FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Manager\\RepositoryManagerInterface`
- `Symfony\\Component\\Config\\FileLocator`

The annotations did not provide the call order. The two Client names are similar and easy to mistake for one object in search results;`RepositoryManagerInterface` and `FileLocator` are also merely adjacent items visible in the current file header. The early notes did not contain enough evidence to determine whether they were on the same anomalous path; this gap is retained.

If all that is visible is import and a class declaration, the investigation at the time usually stopped here. Continuing to guess the next file from its name yields only more words, not an observation of an object.

## 2023-05-25 Review Addendum

The review on the following day did not reconstruct a complete call path, but it clearly pointed out a conflation in the old approach: a file entry point does not constitute attribution of the anomaly.`FOSElasticaExtension` can serve as a starting point for rechecking, but its appearance in the path does not justify writing that the template configuration has already been handled by it.

The review also treated the two Client items separately. The alias of `Elastica\\Client as ElasticaClient` cannot replace the object relationship of `FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Elastica\\Client`. Seeing `RepositoryManagerInterface` does not imply that template sorting passed through repository; seeing `FileLocator` does not imply that a configuration has been located or loaded.

From this addendum onward, troubleshooting first asks "what is currently visible" and then asks "is it worth pursuing": record the input name, object, actual value read, and stopping point separately. Without an object, do not treat a class name as an object; without a value, do not treat a method name as a result.

## An Attempt That Did Not Work

Old notes once connected the following three steps:

1. Confirm `template` is not empty;
2. Open `FOSElasticaExtension`;
3. Explain the anomaly directly in terms of template pattern and priority.

The problem with this attempt was not that the file could not be opened, but that observation stopped at the class declaration. A non-empty input only shows that there is content on the input side; a class declaration only shows that some extension type appears in the file; there is no visible configuration object between them. Using these two items to explain the ordering result directly amounts to skipping the part that really needs to be confirmed.

The same problem appears with the enum clue. Early on, backed enum normalization was listed alongside template terms only because they were placed under the same compatibility window topic. The existing excerpt does not show that they share a phase, nor does it show that enum conversion passes through this extension. Therefore, "appearing on the same page" is no longer treated as "the same path".

## 2023 Year-End Narrowing

The 2023-12-14 version kept the old entry point but removed the overly broad attribution. The local information currently available for direct use is still the namespace, `FOSElasticaExtension extends Extension`, imports at the top of the file, and two declaration locations. These are useful for returning to `src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php`, but do not provide a complete template generation process.

At the time, the approach was changed to the following:

```text
A template configuration issue appears
├─ template is empty
│  └─ Record the input locations for template and indextemplateconfig, and stop on the configuration side
├─ template is non-empty
│  ├─ The corresponding configuration object cannot be found
│  │  └─ Record the last visible name and path, and stop before the object
│  └─ The configuration object is found
│     └─ Check the actual value read and the adjacent usage locations
└─ Only a class declaration or import is present
   └─ Use it as an entry point for tracing back, without inferring downstream causality
```

Here, "stop" does not mean that the exception has been handled, but that the material only goes as far as this point. Empty input does not mean a default template, and non-empty input does not mean an object has been formed. If only the text `template` appears, retain the text and its location; if an object appears, record its value separately; if a value appears, then record the immediately adjacent usage location.

## Old lines retained on the meeting page

An old meeting page showed two Client entries on the same line, with "look at the client first, then the template" written beside them. The diagram was not deleted because it explains why people in the early days always started from the import list. The diagram also placed `RepositoryManagerInterface` in the next box after the template exception, but this was only how things were arranged in the meeting, not a verified call sequence.

The same page grouped template pattern and priority with backed enum normalization. This classification was later marked as the old framing. It can still show how the topics were organized at the time, but it is no longer used as a branch in live troubleshooting. Now, when these two symptoms are encountered, separately record the input, object, value, or stopping point for each; unless there are direct snippets showing the same object and the same output, do not combine the two records into a single causal chain.

## Branches after failure

If the first report from the field is that the template input is empty, record where `template` and `indextemplateconfig` appear, then stop on the configuration side. Do not describe an empty value as an extension loading failure, and do not add a default configuration that has not been seen.

If `template` is non-empty but there is no object, `src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php` can still serve as an entry point for tracing back. You may attach `FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\DependencyInjection`, `FOSElasticaExtension`, or line numbers to make it easy to return to the same location; the record must stop between the input and the object.

If the object has already appeared but no pattern has been read, find where the object directly exposes its values; if a pattern is visible but priority is not, retain the observed pattern and leave priority as unobserved; if both are visible, then describe the specific anomaly. Do not substitute an object name, method name, or import name for an actual value.

If the only symptom is backed enum normalization, create a separate record. At a minimum, separately record the input value, the visible conversion result, and the point where the failure stopped. If any item is missing, stop at the last snippet, without attributing the conversion to the extension just because the extension file is already open, and without linking the enum issue to the template object just because the template input is nonempty.

## Review excerpt: entry point, object, value

The year-end review in 2023 left a brief assessment: "A path can point the way, but it cannot stand in for an object." This statement did not call for filling in the entire engineering chain, only for troubleshooting records to be truthful about the level currently visible.

Therefore, when you see a class declaration, record a class declaration; when you see an import, record an import; when you see input, record input. Only continue tracing the values it exposes when the same configuration object can be matched across adjacent snippets. Apply the same approach to the two Client entries: first confirm the names and purposes in the current snippet, without deciding in advance which one is "responsible for templates."

This assessment also explains why `FileLocator` cannot directly become the next step. It is a dependency visible in the file header, and the current material does not establish its specific relationship to any template configuration. Writing it up as "the configuration has been found" would add a layer of observation to the historical record that does not exist in the actual investigation.

## Current object verification

Only use the following object requirements once troubleshooting reaches "a configuration object is already available":

IndexTemplateConfig accepts ordered non-empty index_patterns and exposes the declared patterns through getIndexPatterns while retaining an integer priority through getPriority.

This requirement appears after the old entry point, failed approaches, and supplemental review notes to avoid using object rules in place of the earlier work of locating the object. During the investigation, separately record the `index_patterns` in the input, the patterns actually shown by the object, its priority, and the immediately adjacent call result. Seeing only the name `getIndexPatterns` or `getPriority` does not mean the result of this invocation has been obtained.

If `index_patterns` is empty, do not describe the object as already having a usable template configuration. If only patterns are visible, retain those observations and mark priority as not observed. Only when declared patterns and integer priority both have corresponding visible values should you continue recording anomalous behavior in template pattern and priority. "Ordered" and "non-empty" are both requirements for the object; a single pattern name cannot stand in for them.

This is also the final narrowing of the earliest instruction to "check the extension first": the extension file is still a useful entry point, but the object currently being checked is `IndexTemplateConfig`, and the checks cover patterns and priority. Troubleshooting can move to the next step only when the entry point, object, and values are each present.

## Recording the enum branch in practice

backed enum normalization does not use the verification statement for template objects. The only thing it shares with the template branch is the recording order: first retain the input, then the last visible object or result, and finally mark where execution stopped on failure.

If the same feedback mentions both templates and enum, first write two local records. The template row proceeds through `template`, the configuration object, pattern, and priority; the enum row proceeds through the enum input, the visible conversion result, and the failure location. There is currently no material linking the two to the same stage, so do not use the same extension entry point to fill a gap in either record.

If direct excerpts later appear showing the same input, the same object, and the same output, add the relationship to this page then. The current page does not commit to such a relationship in advance, nor does it treat the shared theme of compatibility window as an execution sequence.

## Adjacent issues not yet split out

The actual usage location of `FileLocator` has still not been added to this record. For now, it can be retained as navigation at the top of the file, but do not state that a template configuration has already been located through it. The specific usage relationship between the two Client objects should also only be recorded once actual excerpts appear; similar names alone are not enough to determine the relationship between the objects.

Another unresolved item is which portion of local output should be saved when the template object has already been formed but the result appears only in other output. There is currently no frozen output sample. When you encounter such a case, first retain the actual input, object, and values, along with the last location that can still be opened; do not fill gaps with method names or default values.

DOC-13 documents the compatibility verification path for raw finder interfaces and modern DBAL listener registration. It can serve as navigation to an adjacent topic, but is not evidence for this page's template objects or enum results. Keep the two paths separate.

## Old appendix: the quick sequence at the time

> 1. Search for `template`.
> 2. If you see a null value, return to the configuration.
> 3. If you see a non-null value, open `FOSElasticaExtension`.
> 4. Guess the next location based on the import list.

**Deprecated.** Step 4 is no longer used as a troubleshooting action. Step 3 can still be used for navigation, but cannot establish the cause on its own. The appendix is retained, as early records did repeatedly lead to `src/DependencyInjection/FOSElasticaExtension.php`, and deleting it would erase the history of how this entry point was established.

There is also still a line next to the appendix saying "Template exceptions and enum exceptions can be examined together". This statement only reflects the classification used in earlier meetings. Current procedures collect the inputs, objects and values or stopping points separately; when no direct snippets are available, do not link the two types of exceptions into a single path.

# Finder Interface Compatibility Migration

This record initially treated raw finder interfaces as a one-off integration at the call site, leaving modern DBAL listener registration for a separate investigation later. That split is still useful for rollback, but the first version's claim that the finder needs no changes no longer applies. The old paragraphs are retained because later investigations of similar issues still start by following that mistaken assumption to the same file.

The review still starts at `src/Finder/TransformedFinder.php`. Here, `Elastica\Query` and `Elastica\SearchableInterface` are visible, right next to `FantaPaginatorAdapter` and `HybridPaginatorAdapter`. They are a reminder to treat query results, searchable objects, and pagination paths separately during migration. Just because a call ultimately gets raw results does not mean both pagination adapters should also be replaced together.

## Retained Old Procedure

The old version required us to "wire up raw at the call site first, then decide whether the finder needs adjustment." That sequence once helped keep listener issues out of finder changes, but it overlooked ownership of the interfaces themselves. If you still follow the old version and only add branches at the call sites, calls to Fang Ke can look unchanged for a while, but code that needs raw or paginated raw results will continue to bypass the finder's public capabilities.

The old version also deferred listener registration until after finder verification. This did not mean the listener was unimportant; there was no basis at the time for handling both in the same change. That constraint still applies: do not use passing finder checks as a substitute for checking modern DBAL listener registration.

## Migration Order for This Change

First, list whether each affected call retains transformed results, raw results, or paginated results. Leave result handling for existing transformed calls unchanged as part of interface compatibility work; this is the baseline for restoring the old path.

Next, confirm the finder's interface surface rather than just adding temporary branches at the call sites. The conclusion after review is: TransformedFinder implements RawFinderInterface and PaginatedRawFinderInterface while retaining its transformed finder behavior.

This statement corrects two earlier misreadings. First, raw support is not a patch available only through bypass calls. Second, adding raw and paginated raw interfaces does not mean abandoning the transformed finder's existing behavior. During migration, therefore, retain transformed calls, then route calls that actually need raw results through the corresponding interfaces. Do not convert all calls to raw just to make them uniform.

Check paginated calls separately. Both adapters appear nearby in the file; this migration record can only require checking which one the call uses. There is no supporting material for designating `FantaPaginatorAdapter` or `HybridPaginatorAdapter` as the sole compatibility path. If paginated results become abnormal after a raw interface change, first review the adapter selected by the call, then the finder's interface integration. Do not change the listener first.

```text
Old: caller ── transformed finder ── transformed results

New: original caller ── transformed finder ── transformed results
    raw caller ── raw / paginated raw interfaces ── raw results
```

## Separate listener Handling

modern DBAL listener registration remains a separate verification track. When migrating the finder, only confirm that the two have not been combined into a single change. Check registration itself starting from the pre-call state; whether it leaves any additional visible changes after completion must be confirmed at the actual listener entry point. This step remains in the finder document to stop the old troubleshooting habit of attributing all compatibility issues to `TransformedFinder`.

This also explains why "the finder supports raw" cannot establish that listener registration is complete. The former concerns the finder's interfaces and behavior; the latter concerns registration of the DBAL listener. They may arise in the same compatibility window, but migration and rollback must be handled separately for each.

## Restore the Old Path

If new raw or paginated raw calls change the behavior of the original transformed calls, first remove the interface integration for the new calls and restore the original transformed result handling. Do not replace the paginator adapter at the same time, and do not modify listener registration in the same rollback. Otherwise, you will not be able to tell whether the rollback is restoring finder behavior or undoing a side effect of another change.

If the issue appears only during listener verification, keep the finder in the interface state confirmed in this review and check the registration entry point instead. The old claim that "the finder itself does not need to change" has been crossed out, but "do not use finder changes to hide listener differences" still applies.

Verification notes on query sort precedence and typed template accessor are in DOC-14; they do not replace the raw finder/listener boundary maintained here.

# Query Sort Precedence Trial Run Notes

The recheck still starts from `src/Subscriber/PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber.php`. This file is the reference point near the query pagination request, and `PaginateElasticaQuerySubscriber` is the object name used for this follow-up check; it was not treated as an ownership note for template construction or index configuration.

The file also contains `FOS` (line 12). This only anchors the recheck entry point in the same PHP module: this comparison is limited to the request-and-subscriber side; even though the template accessor is part of the same compatibility window, it is not treated as a variable in the sort experiment.

Earlier notes reduced the question to "Will same-named fields overwrite each other?" That wording is not sufficient: the request-side sort parameter and the object attribute may already have the same name at the input layer, and looking only at the final query makes it difficult to tell which value was adopted first. For the recheck, the attribute value was retained, and the request sort parameter was set separately to `desc`, so both inputs could be observed at the same time.

The inputs were recorded in separate columns: one column for whether the request sort parameter was present and its value, and another for the retained value of the same-named attribute; the output column records only the final sort. This distinguishes two different phenomena: "the request had no value" and "the request had a value but was replaced by the attribute." The material available here contains no results for an attribute with a different name, multiple sort parameters, or an empty value, so those cases are not included in this judgment.

The result observed this time was not that the attribute overrode the request value instead. The configured request sort parameter takes precedence over an equally named attribute, so a query value such as desc wins over the attribute value.

This also corrects the order of checks in the initial draft. The initial draft first focused on whether the attribute overwrote the request value; in practice, we first need to confirm that the request parameter has made it into the comparison. Otherwise, seeing the attribute still present makes it easy to misidentify it as the sort source. `desc` is a sample request value here, not the attribute's own value.

Therefore, the regression assertion should target the user-visible sort result rather than some helper branch inside the subscriber. ATL-205 can serve as the entry point for routine integration: reproduce the sort inputs from the state before the call, then confirm whether any additional visible change appears after completion. Do not treat the attribute as the final sort source merely because its name is the same. The test should retain both inputs, to avoid masking precedence when only the request value is set.

`typed template accessor` remains listed separately. ATL-222 only require adding one repository regression test, with an assertion on the user-visible result; current material does not attribute the anomaly to this subscriber, and this sort recheck should not be used to draw a conclusion about it. The anomaly only indicates that the template accessor needs a regression; it does not provide a sample of sort interaction. The two records share a compatibility window, but each retains an independent recheck entry point.

Next time, if we want to narrow this further, only change whether the request sort parameter is present; keep the attribute under the same name and leave its value unchanged, and record the resulting final sort as well, to avoid mixing the input layer with the final result again.
