versions.body:
# AWS Connection Compatibility Decision Record

The first version of this page placed the two names side by side, because both fell within the scope of the 2026.09 compatibility window documentation. The page then needed a starting point for further investigation, and the starting point left by the earlier investigation was `src/Elastica/Client.php`. Recording them side by side was convenient at the time, but it did not indicate that the two issues shared classes, a configuration tree or a call path.

After review, the decision was to keep this side-by-side relationship while separating the technical assessments. Investigation of AWS connection option still starts near the client, while investigation of PHPCR array conversion now starts from the results before and after array processing. No materials support applying the results of one item to the other.

## Assumptions Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft treated `src/Elastica/Client.php` as the common starting point for both names. This starting point was not invented: the earlier investigation records do point to that file, and the file header also shows several useful relationships with nearby components:

```php
use Elastica\Client as BaseClient;
use Elastica\Exception\ClientException;
use Elastica\Index as BaseIndex;
use Elastica\Request;
```

From these declarations, we can see that the file is in the same local area to examine as the base client, client exceptions, indexes and requests. This is enough to support first examining the connection configuration and nearby requests for AWS connection option; it cannot by itself prove that PHPCR array conversion is also handled here.

The first version did not describe any configuration key as supported, nor did it describe array conversion as already stable. This wording was cautious, but it still placed "we can start examining both in the same file" too close to "both are explained by the same location". The subsequent review mainly corrected this relationship, rather than supplying a common root cause for the two names.

## Classification Changed During Review

The counterexample used in the review was simple: two items in the same compatibility window may require different ways of observing them. The question for AWS connection option is whether the configuration and client requests maintain the expected relationship; the question for PHPCR array conversion is what content or diagnostics array processing leaves behind the first and second times it runs. The two subjects of observation are not the same.

Therefore, the previous understanding that "one entry point covers both items" is no longer valid. If only one piece of connection-related code is found around Client.php, that can at most move the AWS investigation forward; it cannot also prove that PHPCR array conversion has been checked. Conversely, if differences appear when processing the array repeatedly, the cause cannot be attributed to connection configuration merely because of where the item sits on the page.

The reason for retaining Client.php as the initial navigation point for the AWS investigation is that the currently frozen materials still place the earlier investigation's starting point there. Here "initial" refers to reading order, not implementation ownership. If a more direct entry point is later found in the configuration tree or near another object, it should be added under the AWS entry; PHPCR must not be forced back into the client file just to maintain the page's symmetry.

## How to Handle the Two Options Separately

**AWS connection option**

First check the references through which the connection configuration enters the client, then check whether the option is retained around client request construction. Only when both relationships can be matched through references is it appropriate to discuss the compatibility implications further. No current materials confirm the option's specific accepted forms, default behavior or final commitment, so the name is not being recast here as a list of supported features.

The file's `BaseClient`,`ClientException`,`BaseIndex` and `Request` only delineate the nearby area to examine. They respectively suggest that the base client, exceptions, indexes and request objects may need to be revisited, but dependency declarations cannot stand in for call relationships. If the configuration does not reach client requests, what has been found is merely neighboring files, not a conclusion about the option's behavior.

**PHPCR array conversion**

This item no longer follows the verification sequence for AWS connection option. The first and second processing runs need to be recorded separately: only when both leave the same content or diagnostics is there an observation of consistency; if they differ, the difference itself should remain under the array conversion entry. No current materials confirm which class handles the conversion, and none establish the processed content as a fixed result.

Separating the two processing runs does not presume that the second will definitely fail, but avoids using one result to characterize the entire behavior. If there is only one observation, the page can retain only that one observation; it must not describe the behavior as stable in the absence of a second result, nor treat the name itself as identifying which object is responsible.

## Consolidation Approaches Considered but Not Adopted

One approach considered was to condense the compatibility window into a single check: start from client configuration and cover all release-related conversions along the way. The advantage was a single entry point, but the disadvantage was that a failure would not reveal which part of the relationship had gone wrong. When the connection configuration is not wired through, the path from configuration to request should be revisited; when array processing is unstable, the content before and after conversion should be revisited. Writing these two paths as a single check would let a pass on one conceal the lack of coverage for the other.

Another approach considered was to apply uniform array normalization first, then check the client connection. This ordering is not supported by the existing materials. |     |  |  |  |
```
|     |  |  |  `- Start checking at the usage site of BulkResponseException.
|     |  |  |
|     |  |  `- Not a batch response, or cannot be identified
|     |  |     |
|     |  |     `- Do not force it into the batch-anomaly branch; record the original text and the stopping point.
|     |  |
|     |  `- No
|     |     |
|     |     +- Was it simply that the expected closing text was not seen?
|     |     |  |
|     |     |  `- Check the command's progress-completion handling and the code adjacent to the event.
|     |     |
|     |     `- Closing text is present but the status is still unclear
|     |        |
|     |        `- Record the text separately from the facts after the command returns.
|     |
|     `- Cannot confirm that the output came from the command itself
|        |
|        `- Return to the outer entry point first; stop here for this page.
|
`- Do we need to determine whether the event is involved?
   |
   +- Can locate a direct use of PreIndexPopulateEvent or PostIndexPopulateEvent
   |  |
   |  `- Note the usage site and the progress handling before and after it, then decide whether to continue.
   |
   `- Can only see import
      |
      `- Do not infer dispatch order, success semantics, or failure semantics.
```

## First put the problem into a checkable form

At the outset, common wording is "progress did not complete" or "the completion message is unstable." These two statements are insufficient to determine the next step because they do not specify which situation was observed. In the troubleshooting record, separate the cases at a minimum:

- Progress text is present, followed by an anomaly;
- Progress text is present, but the expected ending was not seen;
- The ending text was seen, but the command's subsequent status cannot be confirmed;
- The outer layer provides only a summary, and the command's own output was not retained;
- When the same entry point is executed again, the stopping point is not consistent.

These are not five implementation conclusions, only five types of initial evidence. For the first, prioritize the anomaly, for the second, return to the logic adjacent to command completion, for the third, avoid treating the wording as the execution result, for the fourth, first supplement the command-level record, and for the fifth, do not yet draw a conclusion from a single run.

The initial draft had directly linked "output not completed" to the event check. During review, this direction was retained, but the implicit premise was removed: output not completed does not automatically mean that `PostIndexPopulateEvent` did not occur. It could also mean that the output was not fully retained, or that the problem was not inside the command. Only after locating the event's direct usage point is there a basis for continuing to investigate the event branch.

## Confirmation of the command entry point

This page starts from only one file: `src/Command/PopulateCommand.php`. The visible declaration is:

```php
namespace FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Command;

class PopulateCommand extends Command
```

The namespace and class name are enough to confirm which command object to read. They cannot answer what outer process started the command, nor can they explain where a particular piece of terminal text came from. Therefore, when you encounter "output that looks like populate," do not enter this tree based only on the wording. Continue looking in this file for the end stage only after confirming that the execution object is `PopulateCommand`; if you cannot confirm it, first return to the place that started the command and obtain the context there.

The stopping condition for this step is clear: if there is no command entry point, no complete output, and no execution record for comparison, the lifecycle cannot be inferred from the class name. Simply label the issue "entry point unconfirmed." Continuing to guess in the import list will miswrite ordinary display differences as command defects.

The file's parent class is `Command`. It indicates that the object is one location in the command implementation, but this page does not infer progress API, exit status, or output strategy from the parent class name. When this information is needed, check the actually visible command code and the terminal material from that run; do not use the class inheritance relationship as a substitute for checking.

## First distinguish batch response exceptions

The following dependency is visible in the file header:

```php
use Elastica\\Exception\\Bulk\\ResponseException as BulkResponseException;
```

During troubleshooting, `BulkResponseException` is an anchor worth searching for first. Its alias is also important: when you later see `BulkResponseException` in the command file, trace it through this import to the batch response exception rather than treating it as another local class name.

But an import does not mean that an exception has already occurred. It does not prove that the exception will occur in every populate, does not prove that it will occur before or after progress ends, and does not prove that the command will convert it into a fixed piece of output. When exception text is present in the observed output, first check whether the text corresponds to the batch response; if it does, then inspect the reference location in the file and the progress actions before and after that location. When no exception text is present, do not invent a "batch failure" explanation merely because this import exists.

### Branch with exception text

If the continuous terminal segment does in fact contain an exception, first retain the original start and end points. Do not leave only the exception type, and do not leave only the progress percentage. The adjacent ordering between the two is the only material here that can help determine whether it was "displayed first, then failed" or whether the finalization was "written only after failure."

Next look in `PopulateCommand` for direct references to `BulkResponseException`. If you find one, check whether it matches the exception text observed in the actual run, then look for progress-related operations or event objects near the reference. If you cannot find one, do not interpret that absence as proof that the exception cannot have come from a bulk response; it only means that no corresponding direct usage was located in this file, and further investigation needs to return to the actual source of the exception.

If the exception text does not point to a bulk response, or the text was truncated by an outer system, retain "exception category unconfirmed". Do not force it into the `BulkResponseException` branch just to keep moving down the tree. The value of this branch is to narrow down the points to check, not to give every kind of failure the same name.

### Branch without exception text

When there is no exception text, the issue is often described as "there was no wrap-up at the end" or "progress was visible, but it is unclear whether it finished". Start with a narrower question here: after the last block of progress text in the terminal, is there any material that can be checked at the command level? If not, stop at missing output; if so, check whether the record for that run can confirm that the command is still executing, has returned, or was interrupted by an outer layer.

Without direct evidence, do not write "the command did not complete". This page also does not treat "no exception" as success. The absence of exception text near the end may reflect a normal path, truncated output, an outer layer capturing only part of the content, or other circumstances that have not yet been confirmed. The current file-based findings are not enough to rule out these possibilities.

## Event objects are not synonymous with completion signals

`PopulateCommand.php` also shows two event dependencies:

```php
use FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Event\\PreIndexPopulateEvent;
use FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Event\\PostIndexPopulateEvent;
```

They point to the two pre- and post-populate event objects as things to check. Here, do not describe `PreIndexPopulateEvent` as "start succeeded", and do not describe `PostIndexPopulateEvent` as "end succeeded". The import list only confirms that the command file has a direct dependency on these two types; the dispatch points, conditions, listeners, and actual effects after the events must all be assessed at usage sites that can be located.

When the issue occurs near completion, prioritize finding usages of `PostIndexPopulateEvent`. This is not because its name alone is enough to draw a conclusion, but because it is the only visible object in the current file with an explicit post-populate meaning. After finding its usage sites, read them in the following order:

1. First check whether there is exception handling or an early exit path before the usage site. If so, do not assume that every execution will reach that point.
2. Then check whether the usage site and the progress-related code are adjacent. If not, do not state in the record that the event "drives" progress.
3. If you can see wrap-up actions after the event is used, record their relative order; if not, stay within the scope of the current file.
4. If the observed output only shows a single line of closing text, you still cannot equate that line with the event having completed.

For `PreIndexPopulateEvent`, its main purpose is to help rule out the possibility that "the problem had actually already arisen at the initial stage". If its direct use can be located, but no direct match has been found for `PostIndexPopulateEvent`, simply record these two facts. Do not infer from the existence of the earlier object that the later object must be missing.

### Stop conditions for the event branch

Stop making judgments about event semantics in any of the following situations:

- Only two instances of `use` are visible, and no direct use has been found;
- The object name has been found, but no terminal excerpt is available on site for comparison;
- A progress action has been found, but its order relative to the event use cannot be determined;
- The exception clearly occurred earlier during batch response processing;
- The output comes from an outer wrapper, and it cannot be confirmed whether the command output has been preserved in full.

Stopping does not mean closing the issue. It means the current material only supports "the event usage sites need to be inspected", not "an event was omitted" or "an event caused an abnormal completion message".

## Consider progress and command return separately

Progress-related text is useful for describing what the user saw at the time, but should not be used on its own to describe whether execution has finished. Troubleshooting records should ideally be split into two columns: one for progress changes in the original terminal text, and the other for command status that can be confirmed. If there is no material for the second column, leave it blank, and do not substitute "progress reached the end".

For example, if an excerpt contains what appears to be the final progress text, the record should say "This text was seen; the subsequent command status has not been confirmed", rather than "The command completed successfully". Conversely, if an exception has already appeared before wrap-up, also write "The exception appeared before or after this text", and do not merge the exception and the progress action into a single conclusion that omits their order.

This distinction is the main boundary added in this review. The initial draft described the issue too much in terms of its output behavior, making it easy for subsequent investigators to go straight to checking events when exception text was missing. The requirement now is to preserve continuous text first, then decide whether to investigate the exception or event adjacency. This does not add any new runtime conclusions, but simply avoids mixing material from different levels.

## Actionable format for on-site records

When a case requires further investigation, the record can be brief, but it should retain the actual content rather than a summary:

```text
Entry point: PopulateCommand / Confirmed or unconfirmed
Terminal excerpt: Preserve continuous original text
Exception: Present / Absent / Incomplete text
BulkResponseException: Direct use located / Not located / Investigation not started
PreIndexPopulateEvent: Direct use located / Only import seen / Investigation not started
PostIndexPopulateEvent: Direct use located / Only import seen / Investigation not started
Progress wrap-up: Seen / Not seen / Incomplete output
Subsequent command status: Confirmed / Unconfirmed
```

This does not mean every field must be filled in every time. If only a terminal excerpt is available, fill in only the first few items and stop; if you have already located the exception usage site, add the exception and the adjacent actions. Do not write "Only import seen" as "Dispatched" just to complete the table, and do not write "Investigation not started" as "Absent".

For recurrences that stop at different points, retain the original text for each occurrence separately. Different stopping points alone only indicate that the behavior has not stabilized, not that the command code contains random branches. Only when you can progressively narrow down the differences using the same entry point and the same type of evidence is it worth continuing to compare adjacent code within `PopulateCommand`.

## Reading order within this file

Once the entry point has been confirmed and there is enough evidence, read this file in the following order to avoid jumping straight from names to conclusions:

1. Start at `class PopulateCommand extends Command` and locate the implementation adjacent to the exception or progress text from that occurrence.
2. If the incident includes a batch response exception, then check direct references to `BulkResponseException`; if there is no matching exception, skip this step and do not assume one exists.
3. Check whether there are any early returns, throws, or other actions near the exception references that would change the subsequent path. If this cannot be confirmed, write "path not confirmed" in the record.
4. Next, check direct uses of `PreIndexPopulateEvent` and `PostIndexPopulateEvent` and record the visible adjacent code for each, without treating an import as a usage site.
5. Only then compare the relative positions of the progress completion handling and these usage sites. Adjacency does not imply causation, so only state a causal relationship when the code path is clear.

This sequence is appropriate for the current issue because the exception, events, and progress object are all near a single command file. It is not suitable for determining the listener's business behavior, nor is it a substitute for reading `IndexManager` separately. The `use FOS\\ElasticaBundle\\Index\\IndexManager;` at the top of the file indicates that this object is also a direct dependency of the command; if the issue at hand has shifted to the behavior of the index management object itself, start a separate record rather than mixing it into the assessment of progress completion.

## Two branches that are easy to take by mistake

**Treating batch response exceptions as the only explanation.** The presence of `BulkResponseException` makes this direction worth checking first, but when there is no exception text in the terminal, it is only a search target. If you assert outright that "the missing finalization is caused by the batch response", subsequent investigation will skip event usage sites and outer-level output, two avenues that have not yet been ruled out.

**Treating the post-event as the only completion marker.** The name of `PostIndexPopulateEvent` is closely related to the current issue, but the available evidence provides neither its dispatch conditions nor the effects of its listeners. During troubleshooting, you can prioritize reading it in the completion phase, but you must not turn "a certain line of output was not seen" into "the post-event was not dispatched".

Another more subtle wrong turn: treating every import in the command file as a participant in the current failure. The fact that `IndexManager`, the two event objects, and the batch exception appear in the same file header only shows that this class depends on these types. The objects that actually need to be included in this incident record should be those encountered in the observed text or at direct use sites.

## When to Return to the Outer Layer

If any of the following occurs, do not drill down further on this page:

- The execution target cannot be confirmed to be `PopulateCommand`;
- The terminal excerpt was captured by a wrapper script, task platform, or another entry point, and the command's own output was not retained;
- The exception text already points to an object outside the current file, and no corresponding direct use can be found in this file;
- Only a paraphrase of "it failed" or "the progress is wrong" is provided;
- You need to assess index management, template, or listener behavior, but there is no adjacent code within the command to compare against.

When returning to the outer layer, carry only three things: the complete terminal excerpt, the confirmed command entry point, and the names of objects already located or not yet located in this file. Do not attach conclusions such as "event missing" or "batch exception handled" that lack direct evidence.

## Determinations Retained After Review

This review did not establish any one fixed failure mechanism. What can be retained with confidence is the troubleshooting order: first confirm continuous output and the command entry point; when there is an exception, investigate the direct use site for `BulkResponseException`; when there is no exception but the ending behavior is suspicious, check whether progress finalization and the direct use site for `PostIndexPopulateEvent` are adjacent; when there are only import statements, stop making judgments about order and semantics.

The earlier record's "near the end, look at events first" can still serve as a quick entry point, but it must now come with one condition: first rule out any exception text that has already appeared. Otherwise, the batch-response branch will be mistakenly treated as a progress-display issue, and the conclusions left afterward will no longer be traceable back.

The parts not yet confirmed remain here: how `PopulateCommand` actually handles progress completion internally, on which paths the two events are used, and whether `BulkResponseException` and the ending phase are on the same execution path. The next time reproducible raw output is available, continue from the corresponding branch; there is no need to rewrite this tree.

# Interval Scalar Normalization Decision

In the 2026.09 compatibility window, once interval scalar normalization was raised as a separate issue, two distinct questions were particularly easy to conflate: whether the input values themselves needed cleanup, and whether the same interpretation was preserved when converting the model to an Elastica document. This decision first pins down where to investigate and make changes, to keep a compatibility check from expanding into a cleanup of all scalar fields.

Review of the existing code starts at `src/Transformer/ModelToElasticaAutoTransformer.php`. In that file, you can locate the type declaration for `FOS` (line 12), as well as `ModelToElasticaAutoTransformer` (line 25). The former is only a location marker in the file; the latter provides the first entry point for tracing the model-to-Elastica connection. This entry point is sufficient for this check, but the class name does not justify attributing the origins of all interval fields to the converter.

## Options considered at the time

- Treat interval scalar as an upstream model construction issue. This appears to limit the scope of changes, but would leave interpretation before document generation on the caller side; that assumption also does not show whether adjacent fields already depend on the converter's existing behavior.
- Check normalization at the conversion boundary first. Follow `ModelToElasticaAutoTransformer.php` to the existing test entry point, and retain the affected units and adjacent unchanged units separately. If the two sample groups cannot be distinguished here, check the upstream model values next rather than starting with bulk adjustments.

The decision is to use the second approach. This is not because the converter necessarily owns all input semantics, but because the compatibility window requires first confirming the scalar form that the document side actually receives. Get regression evidence for this segment first; if values are later found to have already changed at an earlier stage, it will still be possible to tell whether the difference came from input construction or from the conversion process.

## Scope of this check

The normalization check covers only the interval scalar path; do not use "scalar" as the criterion for a blanket replacement. Adjacent unchanged units must be retained alongside affected units: the former are used to check whether the changes have gone beyond interval handling, and the latter to confirm that the issue has not been masked by an overly narrow set of test samples. Output from the test entry point should be attached alongside the specific change or regression record; this decision record does not draw conclusions from results that have not yet been obtained.

The declaration of `FOS` is retained as a reference point for reading the code, not as a basis for assigning responsibility. If later investigation finds that normalization occurs on the model construction side, this decision still requires retaining samples at the converter, because that is where the Elastica document form is checked.

## Where to start the recheck

First open `ModelToElasticaAutoTransformer.php` and confirm the local conversion point that interval scalar passes through; then run the existing interval scalar normalization test entry point and inspect the affected units and adjacent unchanged units side by side. If the test provides evidence for only one of the sample groups, limit the conclusion to the covered group and do not extrapolate to other model fields.

# Async Page Delegation Proposal

This page preserves the original assessment: async page delegation should be split out from `PopulateCommand`. That assessment did not later translate directly into an interface decision. It is still often used to explain discussions of the 2026.09 compatibility window, so the old paragraphs have not been removed; however, their claim that "the command inherently owns every page" is no longer a safe assumption.

The starting point at the time was narrow. `src/Command/PopulateCommand.php` has a declaration on line 38 for `class PopulateCommand extends Command`; the file is in the `FOS\ElasticaBundle\Command` namespace. The populate command looked like a suitable observation point: it sits alongside `IndexManager` and also imports `PreIndexPopulateEvent`, `PostIndexPopulateEvent`, and the aliased `BulkResponseException`. On that basis, the first draft described the problem as "delegating part of the work on a page while the command retains control over the pace of population."

That description left two assumptions unclear. First, dependencies in the file header only show that these objects appear around the command; they do not establish where the page comes from. Second, the existence of before/after events does not indicate which event should be emitted when the async work finishes. The first draft collapsed these two points into an implementation direction, making it easy in later discussions to mistake a candidate proposal for existing behavior.

## Three Options Left Open at the Time

**A: The command selects the page; the async side processes only that page.**

This was the direction the first draft favored. The advantages are that index selection and the command entry point do not have to move, and the trial is smaller in scope. The trade-off is that the minimum information to pass to the async side needs to be specified; the import of `IndexManager` alone does not establish whether to pass an object, a name, or some other identifier. The first draft described this cost as something to "fill in during implementation"; in hindsight, it should not have been treated so lightly.

**B: The command only starts population; page selection happens after the async boundary.**

This direction makes the command thinner, but it requires existing calls to show who is responsible for advancing to the next page. The code locations recorded so far do not capture that relationship. The old draft called B "a natural next evolution." That wording no longer applies: it is only a candidate, not a next step that can be inferred from the class declaration.

**C: Do not add delegation.**

If real calls tie the page, index selection, and event timing together in the same flow, keeping things as they are is more appropriate than introducing a seemingly abstract boundary. This option does not abandon compatibility checks; it rejects creating a new interface based on an unconfirmed division of responsibilities. The first draft did not list it; the discussion was too narrowly scoped at the time.

## Revised Position After Review

The subsequent review only substantiated file-level facts. It did not produce snippets mapping "page," "async execution," and specific methods one to one. In particular, the alias for `BulkResponseException` only suggests that the command has interacted with bulk response exceptions; it cannot establish what exceptions look like after crossing the delegation boundary. `PreIndexPopulateEvent` and `PostIndexPopulateEvent` likewise only show that event objects are available during population; they cannot, on their own, establish the order of events relative to the async work.

Therefore, A is no longer the default design; it remains only the first boundary to try. The earlier statement that "the events can be reused" should be treated as an outdated working assumption, not a requirement of the compatibility window. To proceed, we first need a call record connecting the command entry point, how the page is obtained, and when index selection takes place. Without that record, discussions of moving events or converting exceptions have no concrete basis.

ATL-217 later narrowed the task to finding the real call behind the latest report of async page delegation and filling in how it was invoked and what the user saw. This card is a useful starting point for the search, but the call itself has not yet been saved here, nor have any user-visible results been confirmed from it. For materials from integration testing with callers, see DOC-27; this proposal does not use those materials to define responsibilities on the caller's behalf.

## Check Only These Decision Points During the Trial

If a call snippet becomes available, first determine which case it falls into: the command already has a specific page, or the command only triggers a single overall population run. Only in the former case can A be compared with the existing flow; in the latter, reassess B or C first rather than forcing in a layer just to preserve the name "page delegation."

Then check three points independently: whether index selection is still performed on the command side; whether the before/after population events cover the entire population process or a single page; and whether bulk response exceptions have already been handled before delegation. The answers to the three points can differ. Until all three are settled, the compatibility guidance should not specify async-side parameters, event trigger points, or failure semantics.

The first draft also implied a migration plan: add delegation first, then have callers adopt it gradually. That plan is on hold. Without the actual call shape, "gradual adoption" can neither identify what needs to change nor establish whether the old entry point still exists. The withdrawal criteria here have changed accordingly: if no reproducible call and caller result can be found, withdraw the trial conclusion and retain only candidates A, B, and C and their gaps.

The unanswered questions remain: Is a page an internal command concept or a unit passed in by the caller? Does `IndexManager` perform selection or parsing in this section, or is it simply passed along? Do existing listeners depend on the timing of the before/after events? These questions should be settled after a call record becomes available; this page preserves the trial boundaries from that time, not a description of the current implementation.

# Proposed Persister Integration Testing Approach

This record preserves an integration testing approach that was not adopted at the time. The discussion started from the fact that persister-client-integration still used `raw finder`, but `compatibility window` needed to be treated separately during integration testing. The two look similar, but when failures occur, they do not return through the same exit.

Two options were on the table at the time.

- Keep `raw finder` as the only entry point, adding compatibility checks only around the existing calls.
- Split `compatibility window` out into a separate component, then have Persister · Client Integration enter through it.

The first option required fewer changes and would not immediately introduce a new integration point. The problem was that failure samples would remain mixed along the same path, making it impossible to tell from those samples whether the finder itself or the compatibility scope caused the exit. The second option could keep the scope check more localized, making it easier to compare opposite inputs. The cost was that the callers then using `configuration tree` had not been fully identified, and it was unclear who would still use the old entry point after the split.

This was therefore not a replacement decision, but an idea for a trial that had not started. If the split is tried, first compare only the two paths' respective failure exits; do not document it as an integration rule already in effect. The trial had no start date or assigned executor. While those two gaps remain, "leaning toward a split" cannot be treated as a finalized implementation decision.

The rollback criterion was recorded only to this extent: if a standalone `compatibility window` cannot make the failure exits distinguishable, abandon the split. Whether rollback would mean only restoring the old entry point or also handling `configuration tree` was undecided at the time; do not fill in the missing answer.

The reference location remains `docs/adj-persister/proposals/unused-Persister-client-integration-route.md`. This preserves the comparison made at the time; it does not mean later integration was implemented using either approach.

If this proposal is reopened, first use the same input to compare the old entry point and the candidate entry point side by side: record each one's failure exit, whether it leaves `configuration tree`, and whether the original result can be reproduced after restoring the old entry point. If any one of these is missing, continue to treat the approach as not adopted. Do not treat a single local success as implementation of the approach; when maintaining the record, update only the assumptions, without overwriting the original objections.

# Caller Entry Point Migration Index

This index does not treat a new name appearing in the directory as a sign that migration is complete. It retains client and integration call samples actually encountered during Persister caller integration testing, along with their adaptation boundaries and integration feedback before and after switching entry points. The index is still at `docs/adj-persister/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`.

Previously, `Doctrine listener` and `regression witness` were grouped under the same migration decision, which made it sound as if both had to leave the old entry point at the same time. The draft now tracks them separately: the former is the processing track at the existing entry point, while the latter is the record-keeping track used to identify regressions. They may appear in the same batch of checks, but that does not make them interchangeable.

```text
Old entry point ──keep──> Existing callers
  │
  ├──> Replacement location in the current entry point ──> Elastica client
  │                                                        │
  │                                                        └──> Check index template
  │
  └──roll back──────────────────────> Old entry point
```

## Before starting a migration batch

For each caller slated for migration, first record four items in the index: the old entry point name, the replacement location, whether the caller is still in use, and the input, version, and first visible result observed this time. Here, a "visible result" may be the result after success, a failure message, or the state after the second call; do not treat cleaned-up screenshots as raw records.

If the caller is missing, the entry may still be retained, but mark its status as not rechecked. Do not delete the old entry point just because a new location can be opened, or fill a blank with "migrated" without rechecking it. The existence of both the old entry point and the replacement location only shows that the index supports navigation, not that actual consumers have switched over.

## Small-scale migration

Select only one confirmed caller at a time. For the comparison, keep the same input and observation window, changing only the entry point location. Go through the old entry point first and retain the raw result, then use the replacement location; if both runs complete, also record the second call's state. This lets us examine entry point changes separately from state changes after the first call.

`Elastica client` is a candidate replacement location at this stage, not the default destination for all callers. If a consumer adapts to that location, that provides integration feedback for that consumer only; it cannot be taken to mean that other callers are also compatible. `regression witness` is used to retain the comparison track, not to confirm migration on a caller's behalf.

When checking `index template`, compare the results and errors the same consumer sees on both sides. If they differ, first stop expanding this migration batch; save this attempt's input, version, and visible results from both sides alongside the index, then restore the old entry point. Restoring it here does not declare the replacement location invalid; it only returns that caller to a known entry point to avoid introducing unexplained differences into subsequent samples.

## Rollback

Rollback starts with the actual caller, not with deleting from the directory. First route that caller through the old entry point again, then check once more with the original input. If the old entry point also cannot reproduce the original result, record only that neither side is confirmed in the index; do not attribute the problem to the replacement location.

After rollback, retain the replacement location entry and the observations from this batch. Deleting them would make it impossible next time to distinguish among the three states: "never migrated," "migrated then rolled back," and "caller not yet found." Whether to keep maintaining the old entry point depends on the callers still using it and this project's exit criteria, not on the result of any single trial.

## Completion criteria

Maintenance of the old path for a batch can stop only when, at a minimum, the replacement location is present, the corresponding callers have confirmed, and historical queries still work. If any item is missing, keep that caller in the index; do not use another caller's results to fill the gap.

Persister caller integration testing has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. This index covers only entry point migration for this project; leave records that cannot be classified as client or integration call samples unchanged, pending further maintenance records from this project.

# Caller Entry Point Migration Index

This index comes from a situation that is easy to misinterpret: the "current entry point" in the directory can remain in place, while the old entry point can still be called. When both are present, the page itself does not tell us which one is still handling real requests. For this reason, read the migration records starting with the caller, not the directory hierarchy.

The index file is still stored at `docs/adj-persister/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Its entries support Persister caller integration testing: real call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback involving client and integration are kept here; notes that have not been traced back to a user are also kept here, marked as still outdated or missing. Do not substitute similarly named pages for the real-world context recorded in this index.

The earlier version compared `Doctrine listener` and `regression witness` as two approaches within a single migration. That comparison is retained because it explains why the old entry point was not taken offline directly at the time: the two paths had different failure exit points. This distinction is no longer used to decide where callers should go. `Doctrine listener` is still recorded under the entry point track, and `regression witness` is still treated as a comparison record; new observations on one side cannot automatically overwrite the status of the other.

## The Four Things the Index Must Answer First

Each entry must first clearly state the old entry point, the alternative location, the callers still using it, and the observations from this round. The first two are path information, the third is a fact about usage, and only the last provides a basis for deciding whether this migration can continue. If these four are collapsed into "already migrated to the current entry point", it becomes impossible later to distinguish whether the entry point has been created, the callers have switched, or only a single trial was recorded.

An old entry point can retain multiple callers. An alternative location can also have no callers for the time being. Do not delete entries that no one can confirm: either they have not yet been verified, or the old records have lost their context. Neither situation means the migration is complete.

```text
                ┌──> Old entry point ──> Known callers
Caller sample ──────┤        │
                │        └──> Recheck original input after rollback
                │
                └──> Alternative location for the current entry point ──> Comparison results
                                      │
                                      └──> index template
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate only the sequence of checks that should be recorded on this page, not that all callers must go through the same alternative location. In particular, do not treat `Elastica client` as a one-time replacement name for all old entry points in the directory; it is only a candidate location that has already been used to take on some trial tracks.

## Starting a Migration Batch

When starting a batch, first select a caller that can be confirmed to still be in use. Alongside the index, retain at least the input used this time, the relevant version, the first visible result from the old entry point, and the first visible result from the alternative location. A first visible result can be returned content, an observed failure, or a state visible immediately after the call; do not first classify the output as "normal" or "abnormal" and then discard its original form.

When the same caller needs to be run again, record the state of the second call separately. A successful first call followed by a change on the second call is not the same problem as the two entry points directly producing different results. For the former, first check whether the state after the call affects the next observation; only the latter may reflect a difference in the alternative location or at the adaptation boundary. Without this distinction, a migration batch will collapse different causes into a single conclusion.

Version records must not be omitted either. A caller being able to use the alternative location on one version does not mean historical queries for older versions have become available as a result. Conversely, the old entry point still being readable does not mean the alternative location has not yet been used. The index records only where the current sample actually went and what was observed; it does not infer results for versions that are not represented.

## Moving One Caller Away from the Old Entry Point

First keep the old entry point in place, and do not change other callers. Use the same input for this caller to go through the old entry point and the alternative location within the same observation window. Apart from the entry point location, do not deliberately change any other conditions of the sample. Write the results, errors, and second-call states from both sides back to that caller's entry.

If the alternative location is `Elastica client`, what is recorded is this caller's integration feedback for that location, not an overall judgment on all client calls. If one sample passes, that only shows that the adaptation for that sample did not immediately block migration; another caller still needs its own comparison record. If a sample fails, pause only that entry for now, rather than also rolling back callers that have not yet been tried.

`index template` is the subject of the comparison here. When the results on both sides match, the index can mark that caller as having undergone a trial migration; keep the old entry point and the original observations. When the two sides differ, do not extend this trial migration batch to the next caller. First record the differences and the associated input and version, then return this caller to the old entry point. This leaves an explicit rollback on record, rather than an unexplained series of renamings in the directory.

When the alternative location appears to work but the caller has not confirmed it, the entry should remain at the trial migration stage. The directory structure can only prove that a location exists, not that a caller has adopted it. Even if the caller has confirmed it, maintenance of the old path must not stop if historical queries have not been rechecked; historical queries are part of the closeout criteria and cannot be replaced by whether the current page looks tidy.

## Handling Differences When They Appear

**The old entry point returns a result, but the alternative location fails.** Keep the old entry point as this caller's actual path. State in the index which side the failure first appeared on, and put the caller, input, and version in the same record. Do not modify the original record for the old entry point just to let the alternative location continue accepting samples.

**The first results on both sides are similar, but the second-call states differ.** First stop treating this sample as a successful migration. Add the second-call state, then decide whether to continue comparing. At this point, the difference cannot be reduced to "incompatible entry points", because the state after the first call has already become part of the observation.

**`index template` is inconsistent.** Do not expand the batch further. Restore the old entry point for this caller, and check again using the original input. If the difference still cannot be attributed to either side after rechecking, explicitly leave it as unknown; the index does not need to force a neater conclusion for that unknown.

**The new location already appears on the page, but the old caller cannot be found.** Do not delete the old entry or mark it complete. Record it as not yet verified, and wait for a real call sample. This gap matters: it is different from "the caller has migrated away, but the index has not been updated", and the two cannot cancel each other out.

**Neither the old entry point nor the alternative location yields a usable observation.** This is neither an automatic rollback nor automatic completion. Retain the states on both sides and the version at the time, and stop expanding the current batch. When new call samples become available later, continue in the same entry rather than creating another seemingly identical entry point name.

## Rollback Is Not Deletion

A rollback applies to one caller, not the entire directory. First route that caller through the old entry point again; then recheck using the original input saved before migration. Whether the recheck reproduces the original result must be retained alongside the observations from before the rollback. If even the old entry point cannot reproduce it, that only means this recheck did not confirm the original state; the failure cannot be attributed directly to the alternative location.

After rollback, keep the alternative location's entry, and do not erase the related observations for `Elastica client` or `index template`. The next person taking over needs to see that the caller underwent a trial migration, at which step it returned to the old entry point, and which results were not confirmed. Deleting these records would make a known rollback look as if the migration had never happened.

Whether to continue maintaining the old entry point is not decided by any single rollback. Callers still using it, confirmation of the alternative location, and the validity of historical queries must be considered separately. Rolling back one caller does not prevent other callers from remaining in trial migration; likewise, one caller passing is not grounds for taking the old entry point offline as a whole.

## Before Leaving the Old Path

During closeout, verify callers one by one rather than rolling them up into a vague "green light". At a minimum, each entry must be traceable to the alternative location, caller confirmation, and historical queries. Only when all three are present can maintenance stop for the old path associated with this caller; if any one is missing, keep the old path or retain the unverified status.

Historical queries in particular verify that earlier records can still be reviewed after migration; they are not another proof that the current call succeeded. If the page retains only the final state and the original input, version, and first visible result have been lost, stop closeout. The value of the index is precisely that it lets later readers see why this caller was migrated, when it was rolled back, and which observations were unresolved at the time.

Persister caller integration testing retains its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria. Do not merge in call samples from other projects here, or write migration conclusions for other entry points. Items that do not fall under integration feedback for client or integration can be kept beside the original entry; once it is clear which caller and entry point they relate to, add them to the corresponding location.

## Gaps Kept in the Index

- Updating the index has not automatically made the list of current callers for `Elastica client` complete; entries that have not been verified remain.
- `regression witness` can still serve as a comparison record, but it is no longer treated as evidence that can replace caller confirmation.
- Old observations with no original input or version are not used to declare the old entry point offline.

This index maintains only the migration relationships among old entry points, alternative locations, and actual users. For subsequent batches, append to the existing entries, rather than overwriting them in a way that treats a new call sample as retroactive confirmation of past batches.

# Release Automation Entry Point Migration Index

This page lives under the old migration directory for Configuration · Release Automation and was originally used to look up entry points for the build queues around `.github/workflows`. It packed entry points, alternative locations, artifact versions, and rollback windows onto one page, then gradually accumulated consumers from different batches, so it now reads like both an index and a migration record that has not been fully broken apart. The entry point for the main text and attachments is still `docs/adj-configuration/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`.

"Current entry point" was simply the term used when the old page was written. It does not mean there is only one available location in the directory, nor does it mean that finding an alternative location completes the migration. Only content that can actually be found through the path above is handled according to the original records; passages that cannot be checked against the source remain in their old state, and the displayed text must not be used to fill gaps with new relationships.

## Branches Left by the First Version

The first version compared `transport generation` and `raw finder`. The former kept the original entry point, while the latter separated the failure exits. At the time, the failure exits were not described as the same type of issue, because the failures in the two records manifested differently. The first version therefore left only a working hypothesis: separate out `raw finder` first, then see whether the migration boundary could be clarified.

The first version did not yet have a complete caller list for `compatibility window`, nor had it been decided whether rollback would only restore the old entry point. The old entry point was retained because, at the time, only entry point names and partial records could be confirmed, not whether every actual consumer had moved away. Later edits to the index did not remove this early assessment; it still explains why both the old entry point and the current entry point appear on this page.

The old page sketched a very rough migration path:

```text
Before migration
.github/workflows ──> Old entry point ──> Build queue ──> Artifact version
                         │
                         └── Rollback window

Trial path
.github/workflows ──> Current entry point ──> Build queue ──> Artifact version
                         │
                         └── Old entry point still retained
```

This diagram can show where the entry points are, but it cannot show which side a particular caller actually read from. The original assessment treated "the current entry point can produce artifacts" as a signal that migration was complete. For an observation involving only one trial path, that signal is straightforward; for workflows still reading from the old entry point, it would close the migration prematurely. This page therefore retains that assessment as a historical criterion, but it cannot be used to declare that the old entry point has been decommissioned.

## What Actually Needs to Be Compared During Migration

The first step in the old index was to copy from the old entry point the consumer to be migrated, the artifact version observed, and its position in the build queue. A consumer means a section of a workflow that is actually still reading from the old entry point, not a name that happens to have appeared in the directory. The old page had no complete list, so individual confirmation was required at the time; side paths with similar names must not be merged simply because they look like the same path.

The second step was to place the same configuration at the alternative location and confirm that the specific consumer being migrated could read it. The old criteria did not require all workflows to change together, nor did they combine different maintainers' schedules into one batch. If the alternative location appears only in a curated screenshot, that is not enough to prove that this consumer can already retrieve the configuration from there; the original input, version, and first visible result must be kept alongside the record.

The third step was to migrate only one consumer path. Comparisons used the same consumer and the same rollback window, looking only at that path's input, errors, and second invocation status. The artifact version also had to be recorded with the batch, because the old approach assumed that matching versions allowed entry points to be compared directly, while the build queue might retrieve different configurations at different times. This assumption was not revised into a new rule on the old page, but it is why several batches could not later be combined into a single result.

The fourth step was to keep the old entry point readable. The old index treated this as preparation for rollback: if an inconsistency appeared at the alternative location, restore the migrated consumer to the old entry point, then check again using the original input and the artifact version retained at the time. There was no fixed decision here on whether to delete what the current entry point had produced, nor was an order defined for rolling back multiple consumers at once, so these two items remain gaps in the index rather than steps that can simply be filled in.

Only then was the migration status marked alongside the index. The old criteria required the alternative location to be available, caller confirmation, and continued discoverability through historical lookups before maintenance of the old path stopped. They did not distinguish caller confirmation from being able to find the entry point in the directory, so they are suitable only as a lookup sequence for the old index, not as formal authorization to decommission it.

## Keeping Separate Records for Batches and Callers

This page once tried to record migration batches as a single result: once one trial path passed, the old entry point would be marked as removable. Records retained later showed that consumers in the build queue do not automatically belong to the same batch just because their names match. Some still read through the old entry point, while others merely have content with the same name available at the current entry point; these two situations look very similar in the directory, but they do not involve the same action during rollback.

The index therefore retained three separate slots alongside it:

| Location | What Had to Be Recorded at the Time |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | Where this consumer path originally retrieved its configuration, and whether it could still be restored |
| Alternative location | The entry point actually read by this consumer and the corresponding artifact version |
| Callers still using it | Workflows whose switchover had not yet been confirmed, not directory names used as substitutes |

These three slots are not three completion conditions that can be checked off. They only prevent paths, versions, and usage relationships from being compressed into one line. If a caller cannot be checked against the source, leave the original field blank or retain the old explanation; another caller's result must not be used to fill it in. Migration batches must also be recorded separately by actual file and invocation name, rather than automatically merging similar side paths.

There is also a timing gap between the build queue and artifact versions that the old page did not handle well. When an entry point is read at different times, the artifact version may be the same, or the artifacts may no longer come from the same batch. If the early records did not retain enough version comparisons, matching artifact versions alone cannot establish that two entry points produced the same result. This limitation is a historical gap in the old index and remains here.

## Old Steps for the Rollback Window

"Can be rolled back" on the old page was not an offhand judgment made after an entry point failed. It originally meant: restore that migrated consumer to the old entry point, retain the original input and the artifact version from that time, then observe whether the consumer returned to its previous read location. There was no fixed answer at the time on whether the current entry point would remain; the old page also did not say who should act on which path first when multiple consumers rolled back together.

ATLD-001 later listed "missing exit action" separately. This exposed a specific gap in the original index: the page said rollback was possible but provided neither a rollback command nor a stopping condition. ATLD-007 further required replaying the rollback using the exit action corresponding to "Current Entry Point Old Entry Point Migration Index" and checking whether the old edge had actually disappeared. These two cards did not turn this page into a complete runbook; they only show that restoring a read location once and clearing an old relationship are not the same thing.

The old page's rollback sequence can therefore be used only within the following scope: first retain the original input, original version, and first failure result; then return that consumer to the old entry point; then recheck the read status of the same path. If the records show only that the current entry point can still produce artifacts, that does not confirm that the old edge has disappeared. Without an exit command or stopping condition, "can be rolled back" in the index remains an outdated statement.

A later reminder also addressed the basis for data collection: after the collection strategy changes, trends before and after exiting the entry point cannot be compared directly. This reminder conflicts with the old page's original approach of tying the rollback window to visible results, but there is not enough material to recalculate the two results on the same basis. When replaying the rollback, retain only the respective original records, and do not splice together before-and-after values from different collection strategies as proof of migration.

## Gaps Encountered While Tracing Early Material

The direction of work in ATLD-003 was to follow the revision history of `configuration-release-automation` back to the earliest material that could be reconstructed, rather than guessing entry point relationships from the text displayed on the page. This direction was added only after the old page had provided paths but no complete execution records. The corresponding record noted that the collection records needed for the execution records had not arrived; this gap cannot be counted as zero executions, nor can it be interpreted to mean that a particular build queue never used the old entry point.

Some descriptions of alternative locations in the old index cannot be checked against the source. ATLD-010 required first finding material that could support `adj-configuration`; if none could be found, that description was to be hidden rather than supplemented with a seemingly complete migration conclusion. This conflicts with the old page's former criterion that "being able to see the new entry point in the directory counts as completion," so both criteria are retained side by side: the former is the handling direction added to the cards later, while the latter is a misleading assessment left in this old document.

ATLD-004 also listed the current entry point's target and the person who last confirmed it as items to check. Vacancies left by departures must remain as they are, without filling them with names from other pages. The maintainer map in DOC-41 can help locate the maintenance boundaries of Configuration · Release Automation, but it cannot confirm on behalf of this index that an old caller has migrated away; the maintainer mapping and the entry point migration records remain two separate things.

The entry point paths here must not be treated as version relationships either. `docs/adj-configuration/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md` is the locator for this export, and `latest-known` is only a known export marker provided by the project. The main text continues to be handled only according to the old entry points, alternative locations, and caller records that can be found in the project materials; passages without source-check results do not become facts simply by appearing on the page.

## Later Card Annotations on This Page

ATLD-001 and ATLD-007 both concern exit actions, but the former points out that the index lacks an action or stopping point, while the latter requires replaying the rollback and checking the old edge. They cannot be combined into a conclusion that "rollback has been completed." ATLD-003 focuses on the earliest material and missing collection records, ATLD-010 focuses on not adding conclusions when source checks are impossible, and ATLD-004 focuses on the current entry point's target and the person who last confirmed it; each of these cards addresses a different gap.

ATLD-003, ATLD-001, ATLD-007, ATLD-004, and ATLD-010 are retained in the page margin only as navigation entry points. They do not change two facts about the first version: there was no complete caller list at the time, and it had not been decided whether rollback would only restore the old entry point. When consulting the cards, it is still necessary to return to the corresponding old paths and batches on this page, rather than applying a local action from one card to every workflow.

This is also why this page does not describe migration as a straight line in which all consumers switch at once. The only things that can be confirmed here are the build queues, artifact versions, old entry points, alternative locations, and rollback windows around `.github/workflows`. Maintainers with different schedules, artifacts from different batches, and results left by different collection strategies remain separate according to the original records.

## Appendix: The Old Diagram Style Still Retained

The first version's comparison of `transport generation` and `raw finder` remains in the appendix. It was a working hypothesis left at the time to separate two failure exits, not an implementation choice finalized later. The first version provided neither a list of compatible callers nor an exit command; these gaps should not be obscured by the arrows in this old diagram.

If all that is needed is to locate the old entry point or an alternative location, follow the path at the start of this document and check those three fields. To determine whether a workflow has actually migrated, do not look only at the directory name or whether the current entry point produces artifacts; return to the consumer, version, and first result for the corresponding batch. To replay the rollback, first check the exit action left in ATLD-007; to trace early material, follow the revision trail in ATLD-003. The current index no longer combines these partial records into a single conclusion of completion.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

This record preserves a narrowly scoped decision. When maintaining the public entry point, the team was not facing the abstract question of "whether the old entry point was any good", but whether to proactively replace request-events, the shared entry point, as the compatibility window approached. The initial draft chose to leave the entry point unchanged; the follow-up review did not turn that choice into an approved migration either.

The discussion at the time focused on maintaining the team's public entry point at Northstar Search Systems. The review did not treat a particular file in the repository as the problem itself. Looking up call names in `src/Repository.php` was only intended to find clues about the relationships under discussion: it could help people trace back to existing calls, but could not automatically establish who was responsible for the entry point or the callers, much less serve as the dividing line between the old and new entry points.

The initial material laid out two approaches.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Public entry point maintenance review] --> B[Retain the current request-events entry point]
    A --> C[Adjust the entry point in line with the compatibility window]
    B --> D[Continue observing actual impact]
    C --> E[Coordinate with callers]
    C --> F[Retain the old entry point as a fallback]
```

The two branches in the diagram are not an implementation sequence. The right-hand side shows the prerequisites that still applied to the option set aside at the time; the left-hand side shows the limited-scope decision that had already been made. The review did not approve opening a new entry point first and then using live callers to fill in the impact details, nor did it approve deleting the old path before confirming who was affected.

## What Each of the Two Options Meant at the Time

| Approach | Immediate outcome available at the time | What the review did not supply for it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current entry point | Existing callers would not be forced to change their entry point because of this round of discussion, and the old path would remain available as a fallback | This did not imply that all callers had the same relationships, nor could unobserved users be counted as confirmed affected users |
| Adjust the entry point | Discussion of changes to the compatibility window could be centered on a new entry point | This required coordinating with callers, explaining the relationship between old and new, and retaining the old entry point; the material did not provide a full account of the impact or rollback arrangements |

The rationale for retaining the entry point was straightforward: the available material was only sufficient to support "do not simply switch entry points because the window is approaching". It was not sufficient to support "the entry point cannot possibly have a problem", much less a migration for all callers. Conflating these layers of meaning could easily lead to opposing misinterpretations later: some would see retention as a freeze, while others would see the absence of a switch as proof of compatibility.

The scope statement adopted by the review was:

> Treat compatibility as an observable repository contract: start from a caller-visible failure, trace the smallest responsible boundary, and leave the old path intact unless evidence requires a change.

Here, a caller-visible failure means a failure that callers can actually see, rather than an entry point name, a window name, or speculation about future risks. Starting with this kind of failure was intended to avoid directly turning a localized usage problem into a public entry point migration. Nor was the narrower boundary of responsibility a predefined file location; it was the smallest scope of relationships that could explain the failure after review.

Therefore, retaining the old path in this round was not passive waiting. It explicitly constrained maintenance actions: in the absence of new actual impact, do not proactively replace the shared entry point with another path; when a failure occurs, first confirm whether it actually occurs via that entry point, then decide whether to handle it locally or reopen discussion of adjusting the entry point. The same entry point name is not enough to show that different callers are experiencing the same kind of problem.

## The Deferred Adjustment Proposal

The proposal to adjust the window was not permanently rejected. It was set aside because adjusting the entry point entailed three things that could not be skipped: callers needed to know whether their entry point relationships would change; someone needed to take on coordination; the old entry point needed to be retained as a fallback path. If any one of these three was unclear, "the new entry point is available" should not be presented as "the old entry point can be removed".

This was particularly true of retaining the old entry point. At the time, retention did not mean requiring the two entry points to coexist over the long term, nor had specific switchover batches or deletion dates been established. It simply left a fallback for an adjustment that had not yet been validated. If the old path were deleted before the impact was confirmed, it would be difficult to tell whether subsequent caller failures were preexisting compatibility problems or problems caused by the switch itself.

Similarly, no specific coordinator was named in this decision. The meeting material called for coordination but did not provide a complete list of callers or an allocation of responsibilities. Taking part in the discussion did not automatically make someone the entry point owner, nor did it justify assuming that a particular maintenance area had taken on all follow-up work. This gap remains in the record and should not be filled by later readers guessing at roles.

The "actual impact" mentioned in the original draft also needs to be understood as it was meant at the time. It did not refer broadly to any possible compatibility concern, but to concrete impact sufficient for the review to decide whether to change the public entry point: failures that callers Fang Ke could see, traceable entry point relationships, and an old path that remained available as a fallback while trying out the adjustment. If only one of these was present, the material was still insufficient to escalate a local issue into an entry point redesign.

## Conclusions Upheld by the Follow-up Review

The follow-up review found no new results sufficient to overturn the initial draft, so the entry point remained in place. The review also separated several questions that had previously been compressed into a single sentence: whether the current entry point would continue to exist, whether the compatibility window should be adjusted, and who was responsible for coordinating callers' transition to the new relationships. These three questions were related, but they were not the same decision.

The entry point's continued existence only meant that the shared entry point had not been proactively changed in this round. Adjusting the window remained an option requiring fresh evidence, and neither its acceptance nor its rejection could be inferred automatically from retaining the entry point. Responsibility for coordination was still unresolved; without a record of coordination, no caller's silence could be taken as acceptance of the switch.

The limitations of the initial draft should also be preserved. It described the "current entry point" too much as a fixed, single entity, while the material did not list the specific entry point relationships for all callers. What can now be confirmed is that the review made a retention decision concerning the team's public entry point and the existing name request-events; this decision does not establish each caller's path, usage frequency, or migration status.

Likewise, the status of `src/Repository.php` in this record has not changed. It remains one of the starting points used at the time to look up call relationships, not proof of permanent ownership of the public entry point. If a future issue does point elsewhere, the existence of this old record must not be used to force the work back into that file; if the issue does point to the public entry point, "we once decided to retain it" must not be used as a reason to reject an adjustment either.

## Reservations Still Left in the Record

This decision can help explain why no switch was made at the time: the actual impact had not been fully listed, a coordinator had not been settled on, and rollback arrangements for the old entry point had not been established. It does not provide a switchover procedure that can be executed directly today. Any future proposal for another adjustment needs to bring the failure symptoms, the affected entry point relationships, and the old fallback path back into the discussion together.

If the review can only establish a localized problem affecting a particular caller, the response should remain within that local scope and should not automatically escalate to a public entry point migration. Conversely, if new material can show that the problem does come from the entry point relationships, the original decision only indicates that the earlier evidence was insufficient; it does not constitute a reason to keep retaining the entry point.

This page preserves the decision at an earlier point in time and the issues left unresolved. For an actual switchover handoff, see also DOC-44.

Here, it isn't a testing tutorial or a full reproduction report; it serves only to answer one small question: does the entry point observed in this case actually reach the selected direct caller? If the note points to a different entry point, return to the container location and choose the branch again. Don't merge the two observations into one chain.

After moving out from `FOSElasticaExtension.php`, first confirm that an actual call connects the direct caller and the entry point. Check the immediate connections in the code: does this caller pick up the object that the entry point touches, and does it then hand the same work on to the next place? Mixing the two makes readers think they've found the maintenance entry point, only to end up bouncing between configuration and resource files.
